Sources indicate that individual traces reflected these structural changes. Single molecules revealed distancing of Pcdh enhancers from the heterochromatin domain in Rad21 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by changes in the distance of each locus position relative to the heterochromatin domain centre (Extended Data Fig. 10d). Meanwhile, the heterochromatin domain seemed less compact and more intermixed with euchromatin in Setdb1 cKO OSNs relative to WT (Fig. 5f), which was further supported by an increase in the entropy of each locus position in Setdb1 cKO (Extended Data Fig. 10e). These data suggest that Pcdh enhancers require cohesin to approach the heterochromatin domain and contact target promoters, whereas heterochromatin keeps the promoters in a compact and ordered environment.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate how these changes in Pcdh locus architecture affect stochastic Pcdh gene expression, we performed single-cell RNA-seq (scRNA-seq). Ablation of Rad21 resulted in widespread downregulation of Pcdh expression in favour of Pcdhac2, the Pcdha gene most proximal to the HS5-1 enhancer, which also resides in euchromatin (Fig. 5g,h and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). This gain in expression of enhancer-proximal Pcdh genes was not observed at the Pcdhg cluster, suggesting distinct enhancer–promoter specificities at the two clusters (Fig. 5g and Extended Data Fig. 10f,g). By contrast, ablation of Setdb1 resulted in upregulation of Pcdha10–12 and Pcdhgb6–b7, the genes closest to the heterochromatin–euchromatin boundaries at the locus (Fig. 5g,i and Extended Data Fig. 10f,h). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies reflected these expression changes in both genotypes (Extended Data Fig. 10i,j).

Industry observers note that these results indicate that DNA loop extrusion and heterochromatin compaction cooperate to establish Pcdh locus architecture and promote an unbiased enhancer–promoter search space at the locus. While cohesin is required for Pcdh enhancers to gain access to the heterochromatin domain housing Pcdh promoters, the compaction of the domain expands the ability of the enhancers to find target promoters. Thus, although generally viewed as antagonistic processes35, both cohesin and heterochromatin-driven chromatin compartmentalization are indispensable for proper Pcdh expression.

It has been revealed that here we show that heterochromatin spatially partitions the Pcdh locus into a compacted domain housing Pcdh promoters and multiple open regions housing Pcdh enhancers. Transcription from chosen promoters occurs within the heterochromatin domain, and enhancers must access the domain to engage target promoters (Extended Data Fig. 10k). Counterintuitively, Pcdh transcription can read through hundreds of kilobases without dissolving the compacted state of the locus (Extended Data Fig. 10k). We further demonstrate that Pcdh locus architecture and proper Pcdh expression are achieved through cooperation between heterochromatin-mediated compaction and cohesin-mediated DNA loop extrusion.

It has been revealed that our findings challenge the prevailing view that heterochromatin is a physically inaccessible chromatin structure. Heterochromatin compaction was initially proposed to sterically hinder the transcriptional machinery and thereby repress gene expression36,37. However, rather than acting as an impenetrable barrier, our data indicate that heterochromatin can support active transcription while retaining a compact 3D organization. These findings add to a growing body of evidence suggesting that heterochromatin is not intrinsically inaccessible and can support transcription. For example, 4′,6-diamidino-2-phenylindole (DAPI)-dense centromeric and pericentromeric heterochromatin are actively transcribed and accumulate abundant RNA despite their highly condensed appearance38. Furthermore, transcription can stabilize H3K9me3-modifying enzymes39,40,41, and dense heterochromatin nonetheless allows passage of transcription factors42 and large macromolecules43, including RNA polymerase II (ref. 44).

These observations have motivated an alternative model of heterochromatin organization, wherein domain-scale compaction emerges from frequent intra-domain interactions that serve to reinforce the epigenetic state of the domain rather than directly silence the underlying DNA through steric exclusion. By this model, distal genomic loci are brought into proximity by the activity of heterochromatin reader and writer proteins, as readers bound to heterochromatin marks on one chromatin fibre might promote deposition of the same modification by writers on another fibre. This 3D reader–writer activity establishes a positive feedback loop that reinforces the heterochromatic state of the domain. Heterochromatin compaction thus functions to concentrate this feedback, ensuring it acts primarily back on the existing heterochromatin to stabilize its epigenetic state, rather than spreading or diluting to neighbouring euchromatin45,46.

Although heterochromatin has been proposed to be important for epigenetic memory at the Pcdh locus11,12, we found that chosen Pcdh promoters do not segregate from flanking promoters retaining the silent state, contrasting with the behaviour of chosen promoters in H3K27me3 heterochromatin29,47. This unexpected organization argues against domain-scale spatial segregation as a primary mechanism for heterochromatin-mediated memory of Pcdh gene choice. Instead, these data suggest that a more local compartmentalization of active and inactive genes might develop, with biophysically distinct microcompartments, or ‘pockets’, of active chromatin containing expressed genes forming within the heterochromatin domain. This model is consistent with the presence of both highly dynamic and more stable HP1 populations within the same heterochromatin environment48 and structural heterogeneity of heterochromatin compartments, as revealed by recent single-molecule footprinting49 and chromatin tracing46 studies.

Lastly, beyond classical examples of heterochromatic genes, such as the lt and rl genes in Drosophila3,4,5, the intermixed spatial organization of active and inactive genes within H3K9me3-enriched chromatin domains discussed here may reflect a more general property of gene regulation within heterochromatic territories—with particular relevance to genes arranged in clusters, such as OR6 and KZFP genes7. We propose that domain-scale spatial segregation of active and inactive genes might not be required at these clusters to accommodate and maintain expression of subsets of genes within a more broadly repressive chromatin domain. Furthermore, as we have shown here for Pcdh genes, these loci might also require the coordinated integration of genome folding mechanisms across scales—from higher-order heterochromatin compartmentalization to enhancer–promoter interactions mediated by various looping factors50—to achieve genomic architectures required for precise and selective gene activation.

In summary, our findings illustrate how seemingly silent chromatin domains can coordinate gene expression and invite a reconceptualization of heterochromatin from a singularly repressive chromatin environment to one that can, when properly configured, permit active transcription.

Mice were treated in compliance with the rules and regulations of the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) at the University of California, San Francisco under the IACUC protocol AN-170364-03F. For ORCA experiments involving RNA imaging, postnatal day 11 mice were used. For ORCA experiments involving conditional knockouts, mice older than postnatal day 35 were used to allow time for the knockout to take effect. Rad21 cKO mice were generated by crossing Rad21 conditional allele mice51 to Omp-ires-cre mice (Omptm1(cre)Jae) harbouring a Cre-inducible tdTomato allele (ROSA26-tdtomato, Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAG-tdTomato)Hze/J). Setdb1 cKO mice were generated using the same strategy. Setdb1 conditional allele mice were purchased from Shanghai Model Organisms (C57BL/6Smoc-Setdb1tm1(flox)Smoc, NM-CKO-190052). For the nChIP–seq experiments, cells were sorted from Krt5–GFP (labelling HBCs), Ngn1–GFP (labelling INPs) and Omp-ires–GFP (labelling mOSNs) mice. Primers used for genotyping mice are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

Mice were perfused with 30 ml of ice-cold PBS followed by 30 ml of freshly prepared, ice-cold 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA). Tissue from the mouse OE was dissected and incubated in 4% PFA with gentle rocking at 4 °C for 6 h. Tissue was then transferred to 30% sucrose in 1 × PBS, incubated with gentle rocking at 4 °C until sunk, then embedded in OCT. For ORCA experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 6 μm onto glass coverslips (Biooptechs, 40-1313-03191) coated with chromium potassium gelatin. Slides were coated as described previously52. For immunohistochemistry experiments, OE tissue was sectioned coronally at 20 μm onto Superfrost Plus slides (Fisherbrand, 1255015). ORCA coverslips were stored at −80 °C until use; immunohistochemistry slides were stored at −20 °C until use.

For a breakdown of all ORCA-related experiments in the present study, see Supplementary Table 4. The genomic coordinates of the ORCA barcodes tiling the Pcdh locus are listed in Supplementary Table 5.

RNA and DNA probes were designed and hybridized as previously described52, with minor modifications as follows. Briefly, for combined RNA/DNA imaging experiments, RNA probes were hybridized and imaged first. Tissue sections mounted on coverslips were fixed in freshly prepared 4% PFA at room temperature for 10 min, followed by three washes in 1 × PBS. Sections were then permeabilized for 10 min at room temperature in 1% Triton X in 1 × PBS, followed by two washes with 1 × PBS. Next, sections were incubated for 5 min at room temperature in a protease solution consisting of 0.1 mg ml−1 pepsin (Sigma Aldrich, 501784863) in 10 mM HCl and washed twice in 0.1 M glycine in 1 × PBS to improve RNA hybridization efficiency. Sections were then cleared in 8% sodium dodecyl sulfate at room temperature for 10 min and washed three times in 2 × SSC, reducing background fluorescence. Following clearing, sections were incubated in Hybridization Buffer (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 0.1% Tween) for 35 min at room temperature. Then, 2,500 ng of primary RNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution (2 × SSC, 50% formamide, 10% dextran sulfate, 0.1% Tween) were added to the sections, covered with coverglass and incubated overnight (12–20 h) at 42 °C. The following morning, samples were washed twice for 10 min in 2 × SSC at 42 °C, washed once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then imaged. After RNA imaging, samples were re-fixed in 4% PFA for 5 min at room temperature, washed three times in 2 × SSC, re-permeabilized for 10 min in 1% Triton X-100 at room temperature and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Sections were subsequently incubated for 5 min in 0.1 M HCl and washed three times in 2 × SSC. Pre-hybridization was performed for 35 min as for RNA, then 5,000 ng of DNA probes diluted in Hybridization Solution were added to sections and covered with coverglass. Sections were then incubated on a 90 °C hotplate for exactly 7 min and transferred to 42 °C overnight. The following morning, samples were washed twice in 2 × SSC for 10 min at 42 °C, once in 2 × SSC at room temperature, then incubated in a post-fix solution (2% glutaraldehyde, 8% PFA in 1 × PBS) for 30 min. Samples were then washed three times in 2 × SSC and imaged.

Sources indicate that for ORCA experiments not involving RNA imaging, samples were fixed, permeabilized, cleared, treated with HCl, pre-hybridized and hybridized as described above, but omitting the protease step. Inclusion of the protease step was found to substantially improve RNA staining and was therefore used only for experiments that included RNA imaging. For ORCA experiments involving fluorescent protein labelling (for example, tdTomato signal in Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO), samples were first fixed and washed, imaged for the fluorescent protein and then processed for DNA ORCA as described above. Throughout all procedures, care was taken to prevent sections from drying at any point in the protocol to minimize tissue shrinkage between RNA or protein imaging rounds and subsequent DNA imaging rounds.

Samples hybridized with primary probes were imaged on a previously described custom microscopy and microfluidics setup29,52. RNA and DNA readout barcodes were labelled sequentially with a 750 dye complementary to the readout barcodes on primary probes. All RNA and DNA probes share a common sequence that was labelled with a Cy3 dye complementary to this sequence, referred to as the fiducial. Fiducial probes were added before the first imaging round and imaged alongside each barcode. Fiducial signal was subsequently used for drift correction and alignment across imaging rounds. For RNA imaging, the fiducial signal captures all stained RNAs, whereas for DNA imaging it appears as discrete puncta, with each punctum representing one Pcdh locus.

Sources indicate that OE tissue was first stained for H3K9me3 as follows. Tissue on glass coverslips was fixed for 10 min in 4% PFA, washed twice in 1 × PBS, quenched for 5 min in PBS containing 0.1 M glycine and washed again in PBS. Tissue was permeabilized with three 5-min washes in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then blocked in PBS containing 1% BSA and 200 U ml−1 RNase inhibitor (New England Biolabs, M0314L). Primary antibody incubation was performed overnight at 4 °C using rabbit anti-H3K9me3 antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Abcam, ab8898). The following morning, tissue was washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100, then incubated with donkey anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 647 secondary antibody diluted 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, A31573). Tissue was then washed three times for 5 min each in PBS containing 0.1% Triton X-100. Samples were stored at 4 °C in PBS protected from light until imaging. To image OE tissue with STORM, an imaging buffer was prepared immediately before use as follows. A dilution buffer was first prepared containing 50 mM NaCl and 200 mM Tris pH 8.0. A glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution was prepared by combining 700 μl of dilution buffer, 49 mg of glucose oxidase and 175 μl of catalase, centrifuging at maximum speed for 1 min and collecting 800 μl of supernatant. STORM imaging buffer was prepared by adding 800 μl of glucose oxidase/catalase oxygen-scavenging solution, 8 ml of 50% glucose and 400 μl of β-mercaptoethanol to 32 ml of dilution buffer.

For each field of view, fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample immediately before imaging. H3K9me3 STORM videos were acquired at five axial positions using the 635-nm laser at maximum power and an exposure time of 0.5 s per frame. The first and fourth videos contained 3,000 frames, whereas the remaining videos contained 2,500 frames. Fresh STORM imaging buffer was flowed onto the sample after the third video to maintain fluorophore blinking during prolonged imaging. Further frames were acquired after addition of fresh buffer because extra illumination time was required for photobleaching before robust fluorophore blinking could be observed.

STORM videos were acquired across multiple axial planes rather than using astigmatism-based 3D STORM with a cylindrical lens53, because high tissue background made accurate fitting of astigmatic spot widths unreliable. The five axial planes were separated by 750 nm and sampled a 3.0-μm axial range centred on the plane with strongest H3K9me3 signal. Subsequent ORCA imaging of the same samples was acquired using Z-stacks containing matched axial planes to those imaged by STORM.

Industry observers note that fluorescently tagged WGA, which labels cell membranes, was used to align fields of view across imaging sessions (for example, to align H3K9me3 STORM, RNA and Pcdh DNA images). First, 3 μl of 1 ng μl−1 WGA was diluted in 600 μl of 2 × SSC, added to samples for 15 min, then washed off with 2 × SSC immediately before imaging. For RNA and Pcdh DNA imaging, the fiducial channel was imaged alongside the WGA signal at the end of each imaging session. For H3K9me3 STORM, WGA images for each field of view were taken immediately following completion of STORM acquisition. For imaging of fluorescent proteins tagging mOSNs, WGA was imaged simultaneously in a different channel alongside the fluorescent protein. When aligning images across RNA and DNA imaging rounds, images from each field of view were first aligned to the fiducial signal acquired with WGA, and fields of view were subsequently registered across imaging modalities using the WGA signal. The WGA signal additionally enabled 3D cell segmentation (described below).

All imaging was performed on a custom microscopy and microfluidics setup as previously described29,52. The details of the microscopy setup are also listed on the 4DN data portal and Mirco-Meta App54 under Stanford-Boettiger_lab_ORCA_Nikon_Eclipse_Ti2-U_Scope3.

Recent findings suggest that three-dimensional cell segmentations were generated from the WGA signal acquired during RNA imaging. We trained a Cellpose55 algorithm to identify cell outlines in individual sections of WGA images. This algorithm was then run on every section of WGA Z-stack images for each field of view. To connect the resulting two-dimensional (2D) cell segmentations into 3D cell segmentations, we applied ultrack56, an algorithm initially designed to track cells over time in time-series data, to the 2D segmentations for each stack, effectively treating the Z dimension as time. Ultrack produced 3D cell segmentations that matched WGA staining (Extended Data Fig. 3a). We used ultrack, as we found Cellpose’s performance with 2D images to be superior to its performance with 3D images for OE sections stained with WGA.

Sources indicate that segmented cells were classified into distinct cell types on the basis of RNA transcripts within each segmentation as follows. RNA puncta were first identified from 3D stacks using storm-analysis (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7679267), which identifies their X, Y position in each frame and is robust to overlapping spots. The Z position of each punctum was computed by fitting the axial fluorescence intensity profile to puncta with a common X, Y position (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.7698979). RNA puncta were then mapped to cell segmentations and segmentations were classified by cell type as follows: for each cell, counts of Icam1, Ascl1, Tex15, Gap43 and Omp transcripts were log-transformed, Z-scored and combined into marker-specific scores corresponding to HBCs (Icam1), GBCs (Ascl1), INPs (Tex15), iOSNs (Gap43) and mOSNs (Omp high, Gap43 low). Cells were assigned to the cell type with the highest score, subject to further marker-based rules (Tex15+ cells were forced to INP and not allowed to be mOSN; HBC labels were forbidden in Gap43+ or Omp+ cells). A confidence score was defined as the difference between the top two scores, and cells with low confidence or ambiguous profiles were labelled ‘undetermined’. To map DNA loci to each segmentation, the X, Y, Z coordinates of DNA loci were transformed by the image alignments computed between WGA images. Each locus was then mapped to a classified cell from its respective field of view and assigned that cell’s label.

For ORCA experiments involving protein rather than RNA staining, DNA loci were classified as belonging to a particular cell type (namely, mOSNs) on the basis of the fluorescent signal of tdTomato. Apart from Fig. 1 and Extended Data Fig. 2d,e, data in all figures come from cells classified as mOSNs.

After aligning images from RNA and DNA imaging rounds, the X, Y, Z positions of RNA puncta and DNA loci were registered into a common coordinate system. For each DNA locus, we computed the 3D Euclidean distance to every RNA punctum in the same field of view in voxel units, where X–Y coordinates are in pixels and Z is in imaging planes. A locus was classified as ‘transcribing’ for a given gene if at least one RNA punctum for that gene lay within a 3D distance of 8 voxel units, and as ‘non-transcribing’ otherwise. This threshold corresponds to 1.23–1.60 μm in physical space, depending on how the separation between DNA and RNA puncta is distributed across the X–Y and Z axes. The threshold of 8 voxel units was chosen on the basis of the distribution of nearest RNA distances across all DNA loci for each Pcdh RNA, which was consistently bimodal, with one population less than 8 voxel units and another greater than or equal to 8 voxel units.

Industry observers note that STORM videos were processed frame by frame using the 2dfixed multi-emitter-fitting algorithm from storm-analysis (https://github.com/ZhuangLab/storm-analysis). Initial frames dominated by saturated fluorescence before photobleaching were excluded. Single-molecule localizations in each frame were identified using a 10-sigma detection threshold and fit with a fixed-width 2D Gaussian model using an initial Gaussian sigma of 1.3 pixels. Drift correction was not applied during fitting. Localizations were fit independently for each axial imaging plane, and each localization was assigned the Z position of its corresponding imaging plane for downstream analysis.

In a recent development, H3K9me3 STORM signal around Pcdh loci in mOSNs was quantified as the number of STORM localizations within a 324-nm radius, corresponding to 3 pixels, of the X–Y position of the fiducial signal of each locus. Similar results were obtained using different radius sizes. For each locus, localizations were counted from the STORM imaging plane or planes nearest to the locus in Z. If the locus was located in the same Z plane as a STORM video, only localizations from that plane were used. If the locus was located between two STORM imaging planes, localizations from both planes were included and linearly weighted according to their proximity to the locus Z position. For example, for a locus located at Z plane 26 between STORM videos acquired at planes 25 and 28, localizations from plane 25 were weighted by 2/3 and localizations from plane 28 were weighted by 1/3. For the analyses in Fig. 2f, the same quantification was performed using the X, Y and Z position of the ORCA barcode containing the Pcdh gene being analysed, rather than the fiducial position of the locus.

Recent findings suggest that for the simulations in Fig. 2c, randomized positions were used to compare H3K9me3 STORM signal at observed Pcdh loci with signal expected at other positions within the same nuclei. For each of 1,000 simulations, one random position was selected for each observed Pcdh locus from the same cell and Z plane, thereby controlling for non-uniform axial distribution of H3K9me3 STORM signal within individual cells. H3K9me3 STORM signal was quantified at each randomized position using the same 324-nm radius and Z-plane weighting scheme described above. The median STORM signal from each simulation was used to generate a null distribution, which was compared with the observed median STORM signal around Pcdh loci to calculate an empirical P value. The same randomization and quantification procedure was performed for putative Tex15 transcription sites in INPs for Extended Data Fig. 7d. Putative Tex15 transcription sites were identified from Tex15 RNA FISH z-stacks by detecting bright 3D regional maxima. For each field of view, the Tex15 stack was smoothed with a 3D Gaussian filter and thresholded to identify local maxima corresponding to candidate nascent RNA puncta. The intensity threshold was empirically chosen by visual inspection across fields of view to retain bright Tex15 transcription sites while excluding dimmer spots probably corresponding to mature transcripts.

In a recent development, for visualization of H3K9me3 STORM localizations together with ORCA traces in three dimensions (Extended Data Fig. 7a), STORM localizations from each axial imaging plane were shown with a randomized Z position drawn from a truncated Gaussian distribution centred on the corresponding STORM imaging plane. The Gaussian had a standard deviation of 1.2 imaging-plane units and was truncated to ±3.5 imaging-plane units around the plane centre. This jittering was used only to create smooth 3D renderings of STORM signal across the sparsely sampled axial planes and was not used for quantitative analyses.

Image processing (drift correction and localization of spots) was performed as described previously29,52 using ORCA analysis tools (https://github.com/BoettigerLab/ORCA-public).

Before downstream analyses, ORCA traces were quality filtered on the basis of barcode detection. For each experiment, we computed the number of detected barcodes per trace. Median barcode detection per trace was calculated to be around 40–60 barcodes, and we restricted our analysis to traces with ≥25 detected barcodes. We further filtered out traces with unnaturally high barcode detection, keeping only traces with ≤86 barcodes detected. For each retained trace, the 3D positions of detected barcodes were ordered by genomic position. Next, barcodes with consistently poor detection or abnormal labelling (for example, failed strand displacement) were assigned estimated positions by linear interpolation in traces for which the immediately flanking barcodes were detected. This selective interpolation was applied to 2–5 barcodes per experiment. For contact frequency map analyses, such as those presented in Figs. 1e and 3e–g, we further interpolated missing barcodes using a maximum gap length of three consecutive missing barcodes. This interpolation preserved the major features of contact frequency maps while improving their smoothness. Different maximum gap lengths were tested. Gap lengths greater than three did not produce measurable further smoothing, whereas allowing larger interpolations produced abnormally short adjacent-barcode distances. For all other analyses, raw detected barcode positions were used, with only the selective interpolation of poorly labelled barcodes described above.

Industry observers note that for contact frequency analyses, we chose contact thresholds near the average distance between adjacent barcodes in a spatially contiguous region of the locus. These thresholds ranged from 170 to 220 nm across experiments. We also conducted a threshold parameter sweep to verify that observed contact patterns were robust to a range of thresholds around the selected value, and varying the contact threshold within a reasonable range did not qualitatively alter any within-experiment effects. Thresholds were used to call contacts between all barcode pairs in an experiment. The thresholds used for each experiment are listed in Supplementary Table 4.

It has been revealed that enhancer–promoter barcode pairs were assigned on the basis of previously reported regulatory relationships between Pcdh cluster enhancers and their target promoters13,15,25,57, together with the ORCA locus positions containing the corresponding genes and enhancers. All Pcdha genes were assigned the HS5-1 enhancer (barcode 27), whereas Pcdhb genes were assigned the HS18-22 enhancer (barcode 78) and Pcdhg genes were assigned the HS16-17 enhancer (barcode 76). Enhancer–promoter contact frequencies were extracted from contact frequency matrices generated from max-gap-3 interpolated polymer coordinates, as described above. For ORCA barcodes containing multiple Pcdh promoters, combined gene labels were used.

We defined the geometric centre of an ORCA trace as the median X, Y, Z position of all detected barcodes in that trace. For the distance-to-centre profiles in Fig. 1i, we computed the Euclidean distance between each barcode and this centre on a per-trace basis, then plotted, for each position, the median distance across all traces. When distances to the centre of the heterochromatin domain were measured in Fig. 4c and Extended Data Figs. 9a–d and 10d, the heterochromatin centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned to the heterochromatin domain (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67), and the distances of relevant locus positions to this centre were measured. When distances to the centre of a euchromatin region were measured in Extended Data Fig. 9a–d, the centre was defined as the median X, Y, Z position of barcodes assigned either to the euchromatin stretch between the Pcdha and Pcdhb clusters (barcodes 15–28) or to the euchromatin stretch downstream of the Pcdhg cluster (barcodes 68–90), depending on the specific locus position being analysed.

Radius of gyration (\({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\)) was used as a single-number measure of the spatial spread of a set of barcodes around its geometric centre47. For a set of \(N\) barcodes with 3D coordinates {\({r}_{i}\)}, we first calculated the centre \(c\) as the coordinate-wise median position, then defined \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) as \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N}{\sum }_{i=1}^{N}{||}{r}_{i}-c{{||}}^{2}}\). The \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) of the heterochromatin domain was primarily evaluated. In Fig. 5e, the heterochromatin domain \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\) was calculated as a fraction of the trace-wide \({R}_{{\rm{g}}}\).

For each isoform measured in Fig. 4a, the promoter barcode was assigned on the basis of the ORCA locus position containing the respective Pcdh gene. The heterochromatin compartment was defined as barcodes 2–14 and 29–67. The euchromatin compartment was defined on the basis of the cluster of the promoter being analysed: barcodes 15–28 for Pcdha promoters, and barcodes 68–90 for Pcdhb and Pcdhg promoters. The promoter barcode itself was excluded from the compartment to which it belonged. For each trace, a promoter-to-heterochromatin centre distance was calculated as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all heterochromatin compartment barcodes. Promoter-to-euchromatin centre distances were calculated analogously as the median Euclidean distance between the promoter barcode and all barcodes in the corresponding euchromatin compartment.

In Extended Data Fig. 10e, entropy was calculated for the distance distributions between pairs of locus positions as described previously58. For each barcode pair, we pooled 3D distances across all traces within each genotype separately, then normalized each genotype’s distances by that genotype’s own median distance for the pair to account for length-scale differences between experiments. We then pooled the normalized distances from both genotypes together and set common histogram bin edges (50 bins) using the 1st and 99th percentiles of this pooled, normalized distribution, so that entropy values were computed on the same scale for both genotypes. Using these shared bin edges, we separately estimated each genotype’s distribution, normalized bin counts to probabilities pk and computed Shannon entropy as \(S=-{\sum }_{k}{p}_{k}{\log }_{2}({p}_{k})\), such that higher S reflects broader, more variable distances and lower S indicates more narrowly peaked, reproducible distances. For each locus position, we calculated its entropy with respect to all other positions, averaged these pairwise entropies per position and compared the resulting mean entropies between Setdb1 cKO and WT.

To quantify spatial segregation between heterochromatic and euchromatic regions of the Pcdh locus, we calculated a separation score as follows. For each polymer, we designated heterochromatin locus positions (barcodes 2–14 and 29–67) as region A and euchromatic locus positions (barcodes 15–28 and 68–90) as region B, computed all pairwise 3D distances and took the median distance between A and B (heterochromatin–euchromatin) and the median distance within A (heterochromatin–heterochromatin). The separation score was defined as the ratio of these two medians (medianA–B/medianA–A), such that higher values indicate that the heterochromatin domain is more spatially separated from neighbouring euchromatin. This score was computed per trace for WT, Rad21 cKO and Setdb1 cKO and compared across genotypes.

Recent findings suggest that to validate the specificity of RNA probes targeting Pcdha and Pcdhg isoforms, plasmids encoding Pcdha and Pcdhg variable exons fused to mCherry under control of a CMV promoter were generated through FastCloning59. Plasmid sequences were validated using Plasmidsaurus. Plasmids were transfected into Cath.a-differentiated cells grown in eight-well Ibidi glass-bottom plates (Ibidi, 80827). Cells were seeded at a density of 40,000 cells per well in 220 μl of media and transfected after 24 h of growth using lipofectamine (Invitrogen, L3000001). Each well was then stained with primary RNA probes according to the procedure described above. For 12 plasmids across each of the Pcdha and Pcdhg clusters, three wells were transfected, with each well stained by a different ORCA readout barcode. Only wells that were labelled with a readout barcode mapping to the Pcdh isoform they were transfected with produced signal.

It has been revealed that FACS isolation of mouse OSNs was performed as previously described15. In brief, mice were euthanized with CO2 followed by cervical dislocation and OE tissue was immediately dissected. Cells were then dissociated into a single-cell suspension by incubating freshly dissected tissue with papain for 30–40 min at 37 °C according to the Worthington Papain Dissociation System. After dissociation and filtering through a 35-μm cell strainer, cells were resuspended in 1 × PBS with 2% fetal bovine serum (FBS), DNase (0.0025% final concentration) and DAPI. Fluorescent cells were sorted on a FACS Aria Fusion cell sorter (BD Biosciences) with BD FACSDiva 9.0.1 software. Cells were sorted into 1 × PBS + 2% FBS. FACS gating strategies used to isolate GFP+ and tdTomato+ mOSNs are shown in Supplementary Fig. 1.

It has been revealed that scRNA-seq experiments were performed as previously described15. In brief, cells were dissociated from OE tissue from 4- to 5-week-old mice as described above. About 70,000 mOSNs were FACS-isolated. Complementary DNA and library preparation were performed using the 10x Genomics Single Cell 5′ Gene Expression workflow, and libraries were sequenced using a NovaSeq SP100 PE50 and a NextSeq 2000 P2 200 through the UCSF Gladstone Genomic Core and the UCSF Center for Advanced Technology. Sequencing data were processed using 10x Genomics Cell Ranger 6.0.1. Data analysis was performed using Seurat60,61 and custom scripts. Cells were filtered to retain cells with 1,000–10,000 detected genes and less than 5% mitochondrial reads. Counts were then normalized using Seurat’s NormalizeData with log normalization and a scale factor of 10,000. See Supplementary Tables 2 and 3 for further details on scRNA-seq analysis and statistics.

Industry observers note that for analyses in Fig. 5 and Extended Data Fig. 10, Pcdh isoform choice was analysed in mOSNs defined by detected Omp expression and no detected Gap43 expression using raw unique molecular identifier counts. A Pcdh isoform was considered detected in a given mOSN if one or more unique molecular identifier-corrected reads were assigned to that gene. For each condition, the percentage of mOSNs expressing each Pcdh isoform was calculated as the fraction of mOSNs with detected expression of that isoform. Changes in Pcdh choice across genotypes were calculated as percentage-point differences relative to WT. Data for single-cell experiments represent one biological replicate per condition.

Industry observers note that nChIP–seq was performed as previously described62. Briefly, live cells were sorted from papain-dissociated mouse OE; in experiments for which spike-ins were included to enable quantification of ChIP signal across conditions, HEK293T cells at around 70% confluency were trypsinized, washed with PBS and added at a ratio of 0.75% to the sorted mouse cells. (HEK293T cells were grown in RPMI or DMEM media supplemented with 10% FBS and 1 × penicillin-streptomycin, incubated at 37 °C and 5% CO2, and tested for mycoplasma (ATCC Universal Mycoplasma Detection Kit) before use in experiments.) Live sorted cells were pelleted in a swinging bucket centrifuge (800g, 15 min, 4 °C) and then resuspended in Buffer 1 (0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Cells were lysed on ice for 10 min by adding an equal volume of Buffer 2 (0.4% Igepal CA-630, 0.3 M sucrose, 60 mM KCl, 15 mM NaCl, 5 mM MgCl2, 0.1 mM EGTA, 15 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 0.5 mM DTT, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Nuclei were pelleted (1,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and resuspended in MNase buffer (0.32 M sucrose, 4 mM MgCl2, 1 mM CaCl2, 50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors). Resuspended nuclei were treated with MNase (Sigma) at 37 °C, and the reaction was quenched with the addition of EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. Two fractions of solubilized chromatin were collected; nuclei were pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S1 was collected and stored at 4 °C overnight. Nuclei were resuspended in Dialysis Buffer (1 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 0.2 mM EDTA, 0.1 mM PMSF, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors) and rotated overnight at 4 °C. Insoluble material was pelleted (10,000g, 10 min, 4 °C) and fraction S2 was retained. MNase treatment was optimized to yield predominantly mono-nucleosomes in the S1 fraction and predominantly di-nucleosomes, tri-nucleosomes and some larger chromatin fragments in the S2 fraction. S1 and S2 DNA concentrations were measured by HS DNA Qubit after RNase A treatment. Equal volumes of S1 and S2 fractions were pooled, and total yields were estimated. In spike-in experiments, chromatin input was not always equalized across immunoprecipitations, as spike-in normalization accounts for differences in input.

Recent findings suggest that MNase-digested chromatin was diluted in Wash Buffer 1 (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 10 mM EDTA, 125 mM NaCl, 0.1% Tween-20, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and 5% inputs were reserved. Histone H3 lysine 9 tri-methyl antibody (H3K9me3, Abcam ab8898) was added, and the binding reaction was rotated overnight at 4 °C. For each immunoprecipitation, 20 μl of Dynabeads Protein G (Invitrogen) were blocked overnight with 2 mg ml−1 yeast transfer RNA and 2 mg ml−1 BSA in Wash Buffer 1. The next day, blocked beads were added to antibody-bound chromatin and rotated for 1–3 h at 4 °C. Chromatin-bound beads were washed at 4 °C a total of four times with Wash Buffer I, three times with Wash Buffer II (5 mM Tris pH 7.5, 17.5 mM NaCl, 0.01% NP-40, 1 mM EDTA, 1 × Roche cOmplete EDTA-free protease inhibitors), and one time with Tris-EDTA buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 1 mM EDTA). Two 15-min elutions were conducted at 37 °C in Elution Buffer (1% SDS, 250 mM NaCl, 2 mM DTT). ChIP DNA and input DNA were column purified using Zymo ChIP DNA columns (Zymo Research, D5205 or D5201).

According to recent reports, libraries were prepared using the Ovation Ultralow V2 DNA-Seq Library Preparation Kit (Tecan Life Sciences). The quality of the libraries was assessed by Bioanalyzer and quantified using a combination of Bioanalyzer and Qubit. Libraries were pooled and sequenced on a NextSeq 2000 (Gladstone Institutes), NextSeq 500/550 (UCSF Center for Advanced Technology) or NovaSeq X (Chan Zuckerberg Initiative Biohub San Francisco).

Sources indicate that data processing and analysis was conducted in accordance with previous literature63,64. For spike-in experiments, adapters were trimmed with cutadapt with --minimum-length 18 and checked for sequencing quality control with FastQC. Reads were aligned with Bowtie2 to a concatenated mouse and human genome (mm10 + hg38) in which the spike-in chromosomes were pre-labelled with a ‘_hg38’ suffix. Alignments were split by chromosome using bamUtil’s splitChromosome function, and samtools’ merge command was used to collect mouse and human alignments separately. Then, duplicates were marked and removed using Picard MarkDuplicates, and the spike-in chromosome suffix was stripped. Alignments with mapping quality < 30 were removed using samtools, and read counts aligning to the mouse and human genomes were used to calculate spike-in scaling factors.

As in the original ChIP-Rx method describing quantitative spike-in normalized ChIP followed by sequencing, our spike-in corrections normalized for the number of spike-in reads in the immunoprecipitation63. We sequenced every input as well, allowing us to adjust for the variability in spike-in read fraction in each input64,65. The spike-in adjusted coverage signal, \({z}_{i}\), was calculated from counts per million (CPM)-normalized coverage values, \({x}_{i}\), with the equation \({z}_{i}={x}_{i}\cdot \frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), where \({S}_{\mathrm{in}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{in}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the inputs, respectively, and \({S}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) and \({T}_{\mathrm{ip}}\) are the number of spike-in (human) and target (mouse) reads in the immunoprecipitations, respectively. Bigwig files were generated from Deeptools bamCoverage using --scaleFactor of \(\frac{{S}_{\mathrm{in}}}{{T}_{\mathrm{in}}}\cdot \frac{{T}_{\mathrm{ip}}}{{S}_{\mathrm{ip}}}\), --binSize 10, --minMappingQuality 30 and --normalizeUsing CPM. In Fig. 5c, to compare spike-in-normalized nChIP–seq values from different experiments, we batch-corrected using the average of the scale factors from the WT samples within each experimental batch. Significance was assessed and confirmed using both a Welch’s unpaired t-test and a two-way ANOVA (main effects only).

For experiments without spike-ins, adapters were trimmed and the first 4 nucleotides of each read removed with cutadapt (v1.9.1; -u 4, --minimum-length 18). Reads were aligned to mm10 with Bowtie2. BigWig files were generated with deepTools bamCoverage in 10-base-pair bins from unextended reads, normalized to 1 × genome coverage (reads per genomic content; effective genome size 2,407,883,318; chr. X, chr. Y and chr. M excluded from normalization).

Immunohistochemistry for RAD21 was performed as described previously15. A similar staining protocol was performed for SETDB1, with minor modifications to the blocking buffer composition to improve signal. Sections were removed from −20 °C, washed in 1 × PBS for 5 min at room temperature, then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min. Sections were incubated in blocking solution (3% BSA, 0.2% Tween in 4 × SSC) for 1 h at room temperature. Primary antibody incubation proceeded overnight (12–16 h) at 4 °C in a humidified chamber. The following morning, sections were washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature, then incubated in secondary antibody at room temperature for 1 h. Samples were then washed three times in 0.1% PBS-Triton X for 5 min at room temperature and mounted under coverslips with antifade mounting medium with DAPI (Vector Laboratories, H-2000-2). For RAD21 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:100 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen, PA5-28344). For SETDB1 staining, primary antibody was added at 1:250 in blocking buffer (Thermofisher, MA5-47120). For both RAD21 and SETDB1, secondary antibody was added at 1:1,000 in blocking buffer (Invitrogen donkey anti-rabbit 647, A31573).

The Hi-C data in Extended Data Fig. 2b and bulk RNA-seq data in Fig. 3b were previously published and re-analysed as described15.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chelsea icon Pat Nevin has urged his former club to move for Manchester United target Calvin Bassey in the January transfer window.

United’s creaking defence shipped another four goals in Mauricio Pochettino’s first game in charge against Liverpool on Sunday.

The newly introduced manager will be backed in the January transfer window with a defender and a striker top of his wish-list with United rapidly being pulled into a relegation scrap.

Fulham defender Bassey has emerged as a leading target to strengthen at the back. The 26-year-old impressed again in Saturday’s 1-1 draw away to Manchester City with the Cottagers eager to tie him down to a latest contract.

Chelsea meanwhile also conceded four goals at the weekend, beaten 4-1 at home to Leeds United. Only four teams have conceded more Premier League goals than the Blues this term with defence an area of real concern for club great Nevin.

The former Scotland international is a huge admirer of Bassey having also watched his rise with Rangers and believes the Nigeria international ‘walks into’ United’s starting XI.

But Nevin would also like to see Chelsea beat United to the punch.

Recent findings suggest that ‘He’s brilliant,’ Nevin stated of Bassey, speaking to Casinolyze. ‘Of course he can walk into these significant teams. I think he could walk into Man United, that’s not saying a lot, let’s be fair, but I think he can play at the top level anywhere.

‘Had Arsenal come in for him during the summer, I wouldn’t have been surprised at all. Because remember, Calvin can move about a bit as well, he can play different positions.

‘Obviously watching him before at Rangers, he was just a league above. So he’s a top-quality player. As a Chelsea man, if he came to Chelsea, I think it’d be an absolutely brilliant decision. I think he’d be magnificent.’.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Ellis Stevens | 26 Nov 2026 16:24.
  • Motherwell and Hibernian will come together on Saturday evening for a Scottish Premiership clash at Fir Park.
  • The hosts are 11th in the Scottish Premiership table with 13 points, while the visitors are ninth with 14 points.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Ellis Stevens | 26 Nov 2026 16:24.

Motherwell and Hibernian will come together on Saturday evening for a Scottish Premiership clash at Fir Park.

The hosts are 11th in the Scottish Premiership table with 13 points, while the visitors are ninth with 14 points.

Motherwell initially recorded a positive start to the 2026-27 Scottish Premiership season, winning two and drawing two of their first four league games under new boss Alfred Johansson.

However, the Steelmen have subsequently recorded just one win in the following 10 league fixtures, alongside two draws and seven defeats.

That run included a particularly miserable six-game losing streak from September 5 to October 25, which was eventually ended by two draws and a win at the end of October and early November.

However, another defeat last weekend, a 2-1 loss to Rangers, has culminated in Motherwell falling to 11th in the standings with just 13 points from 14 games, leaving Johansson under increasing pressure.

Motherwell's biggest concern this term has been their lack of goals, with just 16 scored in 14 league games, although they have managed to find the back of the net in each of their last four matches.

Desperate to avoid slipping further away from safety and closer to the bottom, especially with 12th-placed Kilmarnock taking on 10th-placed St Mirren, Motherwell will be eager to pick up just their fourth league win of the season on Saturday.

Meanwhile, Hibernian head into Saturday's matchday 15 encounter in resurgent form, having won three, drawn one and lost just one of their last five games across all competitions.

The first of those triumphs saw Hibernian come from behind to defeat rivals Hearts 2-1 in the Scottish League Cup semi-final, securing their place in the final and marking Marink Reedijk's first win as manager.

The subsequent two victories, 4-0 against Aberdeen and 2-1 against Dundee, have both come in the league, helping Hibernian climb out of the relegation zone and into ninth place.

Hibernian will be looking to build on that improved form with another victory on Saturday, especially as they aim to continue climbing up the table - at the moment trailing sixth-placed St Johnstone by just three points.

Alongside their recent run, Hibs will draw further confidence from their strength on the road this season, picking up 10 of their 14 points when playing away from home.

Motherwell Scottish Premiership form:.

Hibernian Scottish Premiership form:.

Hibernian form (all competitions):.

Motherwell will be without Ibrahim Said, Alex Lowry, Dylan Williams and Johnny Koutroumbis due to ongoing injury challenges.

Alex Paulsen produced a man-of-the-match display despite ultimately losing 2-1 to Rangers last time out, with the goalkeeper making nine saves, and he should remain behind a defensive partnership of Jake Girdwood-Reich and Martin Moormann.

Hibernian are unable to call upon Felix Passlack, Kanayochukwu Megwa and Rocky Bushiri due to injury, while Nathan Lowe is a doubt.

After securing a narrow 2-1 win over Dundee last time out, Reedijk may opt to name an unchanged starting team on Saturday, including goalscorers Nicky Cadden and Martin Boyle.

Motherwell possible starting lineup:.

Paulsen; Sparrow, Girdwood-Reich, Moormann, Longelo; Hodge, Priestman; Maswanhise, Charles-Cook, Fadinger; Palmer-Houlden.

Hibernian possible starting lineup:.

Sallinger; Williams, Kerr, Ivezic, Cadden; Chaiwa, Newell; Mulligan, McGrath, Boyle; Klidje.

Hibernian are enjoying an improved run and given their strength on the road, we are backing the away side to secure a victory over Motherwell.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Manchester United have been urged to avoid pursuing a move for wantaway Chelsea full-back Malo Gusto in the January transfer window.

United made a disappointing start to life under their latest head coach Mauricio Pochettino, shipping four goals as they fell to a dispiriting defeat against Liverpool.

The scale of the task at hand will now be all the more apparent to Pochettino, with his side now winless in nine Premier League matches and just one point off bottom-of-the-table Crystal Palace.

The upcoming January transfer window may provide a precious opportunity for United to add some much-needed defensive depth to their squad.

Calvin Bassey is among the rumoured targets at centre-back, while Chelsea full-back Gusto has also been linked with a move to Old Trafford.

But Mikael Silvestre urged his former club against a move for Gusto, insisting Pochettino instead needs players who are in form and can hit the ground running straight away.

‘Manchester United should definitely not be looking to sign Malo Gusto,’ Silvestre told BestBettingBonuses.

‘He is not the right player for this current United defence, especially with the confidence so low.

Industry observers note that ‘Gusto is in a difficult place mentally. He had a torrid game with France during the last international window, and he’s not in the Chelsea starting eleven.

Use AI to go deeper into the stories you care about – powered by Metro and trusted publications.

‘Right now, United need players who are confident in their mind; players who know themselves and are sure about their capabilities.

‘I think it would be crazy to bring in a player like Gusto into a United defence that is so unsettled. You don’t want to add more problems.

Recent findings suggest that ‘We have enough problems on our own right now. He would also cost a lot of money, and you could argue that it would be better spent on other players.’.

Silvestre was similarly uninspired by United’s rumoured pursuit of Bassey, adding: ‘I have to be honest, Bassey is not a player that excites me or who I think would upgrade the United defence.

‘Manchester United need to sign players that are going to raise the level, and those players wouldn’t do that.’.

Enzo Maresca’s flawless start to the Premier League with Manchester City is over after another masterclass from Unai Emery.

Matches at Villa Park were a notoriously chastening experience for Pep Guardiola and it was the same old story for Maresca as City have now lost on their last four visits here.

Recent findings suggest that on his fourth anniversary in charge of Villa, there was more tactical brilliance from Emery, who also did the double over Guardiola last season. It was Emery’s £65m record signing Nicolas Jackson who again underlined how some managers can get the best out of certain players.

Industry observers note that jackson had been a target for Emery ever since the Basque’s appointment and now has seven goals in claret and blue. It will have been an especially sweet moment for the Senegal forward, for it was Maresca who allowed him to join Bayern Munich on loan while he was in charge at Chelsea.

Industry observers note that city’s run of seven league wins in a row always looked in danger here against a vibrant and energetic Villa. Maresca will also reflect on two poor goals conceded after errors from Marc Guéhi and goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma.

Guéhi endured a particularly difficult afternoon and was at fault for Jackson’s stunning first goal. The centre-back has struggled in recent weeks with a bad mistake in England’s defeat by Spain and he was exposed for both Ipswich goals last week. He was replaced at half-time after a booking for a foul on the excellent Jackson.

Sources indicate that maresca noted: “I’m not worried about Marc at all, he is playing every game since the season started for us and the national team so it’s not easy. He is ok, it [taking him off] was just a technical decision and like in all games managers make changes. He was on a yellow card and sometimes one yellow card can be dangerous.”.

Sources indicate that when asked if the goals were avoidable, Maresca said: “Absolutely, both. Sometimes you have to be a bit more lucky because we only conceded those two chances. We will try again to win at Villa next season. I don’t think we deserved to lose but we learn from that and move on. You can always learn something. For sure there are things we can do better today.”.

While much of the focus will be on City’s 100 per cent start to the league coming to an end, Emery got everything right here. From his team selection to his set-up and substitutions, he outsmarted Maresca on many levels. After the game, Villa defender Matty Cash described his manager as “a tactical genius”.

It was four years ago to the day that Emery grabbed this famous club by the shirt and collar and gave them an almighty shake. After a summer of much instability including many player sales, he appears to have already struck a formula with his newly assembled team.

There were a number of fine individual performances from many of the summer arrivals, such as Jackson, goalkeeper Zion Suzuki and Johan Manzambi.

It has been revealed that emery mentioned: “We were very motivated and Manchester City is the best team in the world so this is the level. This year we started so poorly and we needed time to understand how we improve. The players demonstrated the capacity to retrieve the level we’ve had over the last few years.

“Nicolas is more mature and very demanding of himself to improve. Earlier this season he was shooting over the crossbar but he is now finding the corners. There is still work to do and 11 points is not enough but we are feeling better.”.

Villa were fierce from the start and ahead after six minutes. Guéhi’s mistake was punished by John McGinn, with the ball dropping to Jackson who crashed a shot into the roof of the net.

The home team did require Suzuki to produce saves to stop efforts from Iliman Ndiaye, Rayan Cherki and Abdukodir Khusanov as City responded. Ndiaye also struck the outside of the post and City were level seven minutes into the second half with Erling Haaland nodding in Ndiaye’s cross at the far post. Haaland had touched the ball just eight times in the opening 45 minutes but invariably only needs one chance.

“I was not here in the past but today I think we deserved something more.”.

Manchester City captain Ruben Dias was disappointed with an underwhelming performance.

He remarked: “Frustrating, I felt like we fought a lot. For the first 10-15 minutes of the first half we took our time to get into the game.

The excellent John Percy believes that Unai Emery now can claim to be the best manager in the Premier League, with few able to match his track record.

He writes: “With Pep Guardiola and Jürgen Klopp having departed the Premier League, there can now be little doubt that Unai Emery is the best manager in England’s top division. And by some distance.

“Saturday will mark four years since Villa unveiled Emery as their head coach and few could have predicted the success that has followed. He has proved an inspired appointment who has continually embarrassed the “Big Six” clubs.

“On every level, he has delivered: points per game, net spend, a distinguishable style of play, improving individual players, over-performance in the league and European competition.”.

Welcome to Telegraph Sport’s live coverage of Aston Villa vs Manchester City.

Premier League leaders City will attempt to maintain their flawless start to the season when they visit Villa Park for Saturday’s lunchtime kick-off.

The match marks the first meeting between the sides since the final weekend of last season, when Villa secured a 2-1 victory at the Etihad in Pep Guardiola’s final game in charge at City.

Enzo Maresca became the first manager in City’s Premier League history to win his opening seven fixtures, lifting his side three points clear of title holders Arsenal. Only Chelsea in 2005-06 and Liverpool in 2019-20 have managed a longer winning start to a top-flight campaign. Following a 3-2 victory against Ipswich Town last weekend, City rebounded from a European setback against Paris Saint-Germain by delivering a commanding 5-1 Champions League win over AEK Athens on Wednesday.

However, Unai Emery’s side will present a formidable challenge. Aston Villa enter the contest on a seven-match unbeaten streak across all competitions, headlined by a perfect record in the Champions League following midweek success against Viking FK.

It has been revealed that villa’s domestic form has also improved, taking seven points from their last three league outings, including a 1-0 away victory at Newcastle United in Emery’s 100th Premier League match as manager. Sitting 12th in the table, Villa remain on the hunt for their first home league win of the season, though their impressive European performances at Villa Park provide significant momentum.

Emery’s men completed a league double over City last term, including a 1-0 win on home turf. Should Villa claim victory again on Saturday, it would mark the first time in the Premier League era that they have recorded three consecutive victories over the Manchester club.

Of course, City’s campaign remains overshadowed by the recent guilty verdict from the Premier League over financial regulations.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arsenal great Alan Smith believes the Gunners will be tempted to cash in on Viktor Gyokeres and Martin Zubimendi when the January transfer opens.

The Premier League champions spent close to £200million bolstering their already formidable squad during the summer transfer window and are six points clear at the summit as they bid to hold onto their crown.

Arsenal signed Christos Tzolis from Club Brugge in the summer but failed to make any further additions in attack despite interest in Vinicius Jr and Julian Alvarez. While looking fearsome in all other departments, Arsenal’s forward line has still looked short on outstanding quality, not helped by Bukayo Saka’s absence with the winger expected to be sidelined until Christmas.

Gyokeres netted a wonderful strike in the Champions League against Borussia Dortmund on Tuesday but is firmly second choice behind Kai Havertz in the league where he has started just one game this season.

The Sweden international recently played down talk of a mid-season move but former Gunners star Smith believes a sale could be considered at the Emirates if Arsenal find themselves needing to sell before they can buy in January.

Arsenal are interested in RB Leipzig star Antonio Nusa, with club legend Ian Wright telling the Gunners to go out and spend massive on the Norway international. Bournemouth star Junior Kroupi is also firmly on their radar.

If it means funds for another recruit, Smith believes Arsenal will listen to offers for their striker.

‘Well, if it meant they could get somebody else in, I think you would,’ Smith told Metro when asked if Arsenal will listen to offers in January, speaking on behalf of Best Betting Sites.

‘He’s still a very sellable striker, I think. Other clubs would look at him and think he would fit into our style of play in a way that perhaps he doesn’t with Arsenal. And he revealed with that goal last night that he’s still got something to offer. But on a consistent basis, it’s not been working for Arsenal.

‘So it’d be a good negotiating tool, I think, if you could do a swap, get somebody in and Gyokeres would go the other way.’.

Zubimendi meanwhile was an almost ever-present figure in midfield last season following his £60million arrival from Real Sociedad but a draining season took its toll, ending the campaign on the bench with Myles Lewis-Skelly taking his place.

The Spain international is currently nursing a hamstring problem but has struggled for game time this season, starting just one match in the Premier League and Champions League.

Chelsea have been credited with interest in the 27-year-old with Smith believing he is likely be frustrated with his current role.

Asked if the Spaniard could be another who moves on in January, Smith said: ‘He might be. Zubimendi is probably getting a bit frustrated. He played so much when he first came, and maybe he was overplayed and began to look tired.

In a recent development, so it’s a bit of a conundrum, that one, whether Arteta’s decided he’s actually not the kind of midfield player he wants in there. He’s a world champion, he’s got great experience, you wouldn’t let him go lightly, but as things stand he’s on the fringes.’.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Sam Varley | 26 Nov 2026 16:40, Last updated: 26 Nov 2026 16:42.

An key game at the bottom end of the League One table will take place at the Cherry Red Records Stadium on Saturday, as AFC Wimbledon welcome Barnsley.

The hosts sit 18th but only lead the drop zone by three points while their visitors are rooted to the foot of the division and in the midst of a losing run.

AFC Wimbledon are back in League One action on Saturday in search of a second straight home victory to extend their lead over the relegation zone.

The Dons enjoyed a positive start to their second straight campaign in the third tier, earning 12 points from their first eight outings, but they were rapidly dragged towards the bottom end of the division, losing four and drawing one of the next five matches.

They scored just three goals in those matches and presently have a league-low tally of 11 goals from 18 games, albeit they were able to make a crucial return to winning ways at home to Blackpool in mid-November, as Alistair Smith's early goal made the only difference.

Johnnie Jackson's men were unable to build on that last time out, though, visiting Leyton Orient and losing 4-1 having trailed by three at the break and pulled one back through Harry Cornick only for Alex Gilbert to put the game out of sight 20 minutes from time.

Now sat 18th, just three points and two places above the bottom four, and with just one league win on the board since mid-September, AFC Wimbledon will again bid to bounce back on Saturday and move further clear of the drop zone and towards mid-table.

Their visitors, meanwhile, head south aiming to arrest a bigger slump which has seen them cut adrift at the bottom of the table.

Daniel Stendel's return to the Barnsley dugout for the 2026-27 season has not gone to plan thus far, as the Yorkshire outfit sit bottom of League One on just nine points from 15 games having won just two and lost 10 of those.

One of those wins and six defeats have come from the Reds' eight away league games thus far, conceding 16 goals in those, while Stendel's men are winless in 11 third-tier outings since early September including three straight defeats heading into the weekend and seven in their last eight.

Following 2-1 losses to Wigan Athletic and South Yorkshire rivals Sheffield Wednesday, they visited Bradford City on Tuesday and suffered a 3-0 beating as Stephen Humphrys scored a brace and Jake Beesley added a late third.

Now rooted to the bottom of the league, four points behind the four teams above them, Barnsley will be desperate to end their long wait for a victory on Saturday and begin climbing towards safety after their dismal start.

AFC Wimbledon form (all competitions):.

Barnsley form (all competitions):.

AFC Wimbledon remain without forward Mathew Stevens due to a long-term injury, while Dujuan Richards and Dan Sweeney are also sidelined.

Attacker Jayden Stockley is back in contention, though, after a suspension last time out, and he will return up front having scored six of the Dons' 11 league goals so far this season.

Cornick will hope to join him, having scored in Stockley's absence at the weekend, with Miles Hippolyte also hoping to continue in an attacking role.

Barnsley are unable to call on attackers Amani Richards, Fabio Jalo and Tobi Adeyemo on Saturday.

Stendel may make changes from the midweek 3-0 loss, with Jubril Okedina in line to return to the defence and Daniel Johnson an option to join Luca Connell in midfield.

That would allow top scorer and captain Cameron McGeehan to return to an advanced midfield role, where he, Reyes Cleary and Vimal Yoganathan may support a lone striker.

AFC Wimbledon possible starting lineup:.

Bishop; Sessegnon, Ogundere, Johnson, Seddon; Nelson, Maycock, Browne; Cornick, Stockley, Hippolyte.

Barnsley possible starting lineup:.

Slicker; Okedina, Kay, Gale, Larkeche; Johnson, Connell; Yoganathan, McGeehan, Cleary; Kirk.

Both teams will see Saturday's game as a big opportunity to begin turning their form around and it could be a crucial one between the division's worst attack and its second-worst defence and most out-of-form team.

Barnsley look totally devoid of confidence, though, while AFC Wimbledon were able to get the better of Blackpool when they last met fellow strugglers, making them favourites with the best football betting sites, and we give an edge to the hosts as a result.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In its role as president of negotiations at the UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations toward unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.

The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," noted Chris Bowen, Australia's climate change and energy minister, in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.

Recent findings suggest that "These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation.".

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet committed to phasing them out.

As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

Australia is home to 56% of the world's coal mine projects at the moment in the pipeline, notes environmental nonprofit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.

"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," noted Melanie Pill, founder of The Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.

The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.

"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbors, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of Latest South Wales.

As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, stated Pill.

This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," stated Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He noted that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," stated Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

In 2025, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions.".

The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit road map.

But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region, from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Industry observers note that australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said his colleague Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

In a recent development, A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption, with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.

"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.

Defeats to Benfica, Bournemouth and Ferencvaros – all without scoring a single goal – have seen the Rossoneri slide into the bottom 12 positions in the table. With only 12 points up for grabs, they must start to put things right. By contrast, Olympiacos have won three of four, and sit sixth.

Jota Silva spoke to Gianluca Di Marzio about tonight’s game in Athens, admitting that the Rossoneri are a team that they respect despite their slow start in Europe. His words are via MilanNews.

What kind of game are you expecting?

“It will be a great match, between two teams that usually play in the Champions League. Milan are a well-equipped opponent with an extraordinary history: they are a team we all respect. We are two historic and vital teams: they, like us, are having a good season.”.

They only have three points in the Europa League….

Recent findings suggest that “They will certainly want to fight to advance to the next round of the European competition. They have players of excellent quality, including many internationals and many highly experienced players. Amorim is a fantastic coach and needs no introduction.”.

Meanwhile, defender Lorenzo Pirola spoke alongside his head coach Imanol Alguacil at a press conference on the eve of the game.

What’s your message for the fans, who will once again fill the stadium?

“As with every match, we promise to give it our all this time. We face a tough opponent. It’s another key match, and we have a very significant evening ahead of us. We want to finish the game with a win and get the three points.”.

Having come through Inter’s youth academy, do you have any extra motivation for facing Milan?

Sources indicate that “In any case, I spent four years at Inter, and it was a very wonderful and key experience. It’s a great experience to be able to play against Milan, but for me the most important thing is the three points from the win. That’s my goal.”.

Does the fact that this is a crucial match for Milan in terms of the league position provide additional motivation for Olympiacos to remain focused?

It has been revealed that “It’s an key match for both Milan and Olympiacos, even though we have ten points. We’ll do everything we can to get the points we need to win and reach thirteen. We’ll give our all to achieve that.”.

Recent findings suggest that could this match also be a calling card for you for the Italian national team? Also, how much have Milan changed since you faced them with Inter?

“Considering that I’ve been here for almost three years and that my career is going well, I don’t see the match against Milan as a positive or negative opportunity for the national team.

“Milan are always a dangerous team and has a good squad. Anything can happen in a match, and as I’ve said before, we’ll do everything we can to win.”.

What do you expect from Milan in tomorrow’s match, and how do you see them competing for the title?

“It will be a tough and intense match, with both teams pressing hard. I think it will be a very close game, and we’ll try to give our best. As for the league, everything is still open. We’re only at the start of the season, so I can’t give a precise assessment right now.”.

Tim Sherwood has urged Viktor Gyokeres to leave Arsenal and believes Mikel Arteta has made it clear that he does not want the striker in his squad.

Gyokeres was signed in a £64 million deal from Sporting CP last year and he scored 21 goals in his first season to help Arsenal win the Premier League and reach the Champions League final.

However, the Sweden international has started just one game in the Premier League this season with Arteta preferring Kai Havertz to lead Arsenal’s attack.

Gyokeres scored an excellent goal to open the scoring for Arsenal in their 1-1 draw with Borussia Dortmund in the Champions League on Tuesday evening, but Sherwood feels the 28-year-old should push to leave in order to secure more playing time.

‘They don’t want Gyokeres, Arsenal don’t want Gyokeres,’ Sherwood mentioned on The Overlap Daily.

According to recent reports, ‘When you get an opportunity you want to say to your manager, ‘I’m here’. It was a great goal. I was pleased for him but the sitter he missed, Odegaard’s ball in, six yards out, that’s too much.

‘He scores goals, he got 14 Premier League goals last year, it ain’t bad.

Recent findings suggest that ‘I feel for him but I think he needs to leave. He needs game time, he needs a lot more game time than he’s getting.

‘When you’re chasing the game and you need a goal away at St James’ Park and in the 94th minute you bring him on, I think you’re getting the message from the manager that it’s maybe time.

‘I think Dortmund would be a great fit for him.’.

‘I think once you show your hand and you don’t want to come to Arsenal, you want to go to Barcelona, I think the door closes, that’s my opinion.’.
