Jensen Huang: Spy row, affairs leave Nvidia without its rockstar CEO

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1089 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.
  • In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier remarked Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.
  • The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Nvidia's board met late Wednesday to decide on CEO Jensen Huang's future as reports emerged of other extramarital affairs — this time with employees.

In a statement issued on Thursday, the world's most valuable chip supplier remarked Huang was resigning as President, CEO and board member, effective immediately.

The firm added that current Vice President and Chief Financial Officer (CFO) Colette Kress would become interim CEO.

Under Nvidia's bylaws, Huang can be removed "with or without cause" by a majority vote of its 11 directors.

The New York Times first reported that the 63-year-old Huang had an affair with a senior Nvidia executive who reported directly to him.

Later Thursday, Reuters news agency alleged an intimate relationship between Huang and a second employee, citing unidentified sources.

Industry observers note that those revelations emerged just three days after Huang admitted a relationship with a Chinese woman, whom United States intelligence agencies believe was spying for China. The woman, Alice Huang — no relation — is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud computing firm that runs artificial intelligence (AI) data centers across Southeast Asia and is a major client of Nvidia.

The US government is investigating the startup on suspicion that it secretly sent some of its Nvidia chips to China, violating Washington's curbs on high-end semiconductors.

Those advanced Nvidia processors ‌are ​used to train and run the large AI models behind chatbots and other generative AI products.

According to recent reports, megaspeed denies the allegations and on Thursday pledged to cooperate with US investigators. Huang, the alleged spy, has been barred from entering Singapore and Taiwan — a key chipmaking island.

While Nvidia's board backed its CEO after the first scandal emerged, market watchers believe the second caused too much reputational damage to one of the world's top three companies by market value.

According to The Wall Street Journal, Huang doesn't believe in formal succession planning, so with little notice, Nvidia appointed CFO Kress as interim CEO.

Bloomberg reported Wednesday that Nvidia’s board is working with advisers to identify potential permanent successors.

According to recent reports, kress, other senior Nvidia executives and members of Huang's own family have been mooted as replacements. The family members include his daughter Madison, a senior director of product marketing, and his son Spencer, who at the moment works in the firm's robotics division.

Recent findings suggest that rumors also abound over a longer-term solution. On India's CNBC-TV18, Jeffrey Sonnenfeld from the Yale School of Management floated former Apple CEO Tim Cook and ex-Google CEO Eric Schmidt.

US President Donald Trump also backed Cook on social media, writing: "A Legend replaces a Legend.".

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

The scandals have certainly hit Nvidia's market value. Since the first extramarital affair emerged on Sunday, the chipmaker's market capitalization has fallen by well over $600 billion to $4.2 trillion.

Nvidia shares were down more than 9% in premarket trading Thursday, after dropping by 10% earlier this week. Some analysts expect the stock price to struggle in the short term.

Nvidia stock hit all-time highs just a month ago as US technology giants continued to announce billions in spending on AI infrastructure.

Demand for Nvidia's advanced chips is so high, however, that many market analysts expect little impact on near-term sales.

"While Jensen [Huang] is the heart and lungs of the Nvidia story…the organization and its leading-edge GPU technology will go on and [his departure] does not change the entrenched position Nvidia has in the AI Revolution chip arms race," mentioned Dan Ives, a partner, senior managing director and tech analyst at Yorkville Ives, a US-based merchant bank.

Analysts see the biggest long-term risk in strategy and execution. After all, Huang was the leader who picked which ideas Nvidia should bet heavily on and got the whole firm behind them.

His sudden exit is also seen as highly disruptive to the chip designer's strong relationships with AI hyperscalers, Taiwanese chip producer TSMC and foreign governments — especially China.

Huang was Nvidia's main lobbyist on US chip export rules and persuaded US President Donald Trump to ease some curbs on China last year.

Huang is often called a rockstar CEO for his leather jackets instead of suits.

Like Elon Musk of Tesla and SpaceX, he was also seen as a key-person risk as Nvidia’s public image, strategic direction and technical decisions became closely tied to him.

Huang steered the organization for more than three decades and was also respected for his hands-on involvement in product architecture and engineering decisions.

He also insisted on a flat management structure, with around 60 executives reporting directly to him.

Huang has run the manufacturer so tightly around his own technical judgment and product decisions that investors may have little sense of how it would function without him.

According to recent reports, at the same time, Nvidia is no longer the startup Huang founded in 1993. The company has built deep expertise in chip design and software, creating a durable moat that helps protect its huge profits, which topped $120.1 billion last year.

Some analysts argue that its central role in the AI hardware buildout makes it less dependent on Huang’s day-to-day input.

China is swiftly playing catch-up with the US in the global race for AI dominance.

While Chinese AI models have lagged behind the likes of ChatGPT and Claude, recent updates from DeepSeek, Alibaba and Moonshot have closed much of the gap on benchmark tests and often beat US rivals on cost and speed.

Beijing is also investing heavily in domestic chips and data centers to reduce reliance on US hardware.

The US has curbed exports to China of Nvidia's most advanced AI chips.

However, this move has only slowed the pace of China's AI ambitions.

Reuters reported Thursday that Chinese AI firms are now trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity at data centers outside China, amid fears the US could further tighten restrictions on advanced chips.

Also Thursday, Beijing accused the US of using the Nvidia spying claims as a pretext to impose a technological "blockade" on China.

The concern is likely to dominate talks next week between Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at the APEC gathering in Shenzhen in southern China.

Amorim has named a strong starting line-up featuring the likes of Mario Gila, Koni De Winter, Adrien Rabiot, Diego Moreira, Goncalo Ramos and the top scorer Alphadjo Cisse. However, what doesn’t help the cause at all are the nine injury absentees, which is noticeable when looking at the bench.

According to recent reports, the head coach spoke to Sky in the build-up to kick-off in Greece to shed light on his selections and the importance of learning lessons in Europe. MilanNews relayed his words.

You’ve gone with an attacking side tonight….

It has been revealed that “In football, you have to defend and attack. We have to defend with 11 men and attack with 11 men. The players know what positions they have to occupy and are ready.

“We have to be more compact, and even with these attacking players on the pitch, we can defend better than in other Europa League matches.”.

Did the players learn their lesson after Ferencvaros?

“I think they understand. We’ve seen videos, we’re working. Against Ferencvaros, we were sluggish because we weren’t compact and focused on the details. In Europe, we need to raise our game and do what we’ve done several times in Serie A.”.

Are you ready to prove you can play three good games in a row in a week?

According to recent reports, “I think we have to be a great team. To be that, you have to win both in Serie A and in Europe. We have that responsibility. Updated: 19:02 EST, 25 November 2026.

Relive Daily Mail Sport's coverage from Wednesday's Champions League action as Manchester United travelled to Sporting Lisbon while Liverpool took on Club Brugge.

It's not every day that you get to spend an evening with Harry Bamforth and Luke Power - and we wouldn't recommend it, either.

Thanks for putting up with us, especially when the football is hard enough to cope with as it is if you're a Manchester United fan.

Do joins us in the morning as the reaction and fall-out from the Champions League action continues interminably.

Here are the Premier League fixtures at the weekend:.

Senne Lammens' two errors cost Man United victory at Sporting.

CHRIS WHEELER AT JOSE ALVALADE STADIUM: A week into the job and Mauricio Pochettino must be getting used to the madness of Manchester United.

Liverpool showed a bit of everything tonight: possession dominance in the first half, counter-attacking prowess in the second, and defensive solidity throughout (for the most part!).

Lewis Steele was on hand to bring you his thoughts from Belgium.

Club Brugge 0-3 Liverpool: Reds close in on qualification.

LEWIS STEELE AT JAN BREYDEL STADION: A brace for Isak and another from Wirtz fired the Reds to victory in Bruges after their strikes helped Liverpool get back to winning ways in Europe.

Lowlights if you're a Brugge fan!

Normally I post all the goals and crazy moments separately, but there were just too many tonight.

It has been revealed that so, instead, you can catch all the chaos in the highlights on YouTube. From penalties and howlers to disallowed goals and sending-offs, this game had it all.

Rio Ngumoha is averaging 7.8 completed dribbles every match in this year's Champions League.

No player with at least 300 minutes played has done better since 2006-07. Full credit to Opta for this one. One man has done more this campaign, and that's Jeremy Doku on 11.9, but he doesn't have the 300 minutes under his belt.

Recent findings suggest that let it sink in. When we think of direct, unstoppable dribblers, we think of Lionel Messi, Neymar, Khvichia Kvaratskhelia. Oddly Thomas Partey was up there in the standings one season. But those world-class wingers, Ngumoha is up there with them for pure dribbling ability at the moment. It's a long career ahead, and you hope his spark won't be muted, but he has mad a dazzling start. If he can add goals and assists, his potential is sky-high.

Manchester United may have been done over by some decisions, I know, but not all of them were wrong.

The red card for Youri Tielemans? Fair.

In a recent development, the penalty conceded by Senne Lammens? Stonewall.

So that means the next stat I am about to share is a pretty damning indictment of United's season (bar the Leny Yoro red, before you all have a pop at me).

Man United have received five red cards and conceded five penalties in just 17 games across all competitions this season.

Liverpool couldn't have had a better week going into the Merseyside derby than beating Manchester United and Brugge 7-0 on aggregate.

The annoying thing for Andoni Iraola is that Victor Munoz has picked up a knock, and he had to bring on Rio Ngumoha earlier than expected as a result, so that inhibits his options and energy up front ever so slightly.

Sources indicate that but he will be greatly encouraged by how his £100m+ men, namely Alexander Isak, Florian Wirtz, and Bradley Barcola, are melding. We're yet to see the best from the latter on a consistent basis. That's the final piece of the puzzle.

Wirtz is flying now - he has now scored or assisted or done both in seven of his last nine games in the Premier League and Champions League.

Everton are having a good season and will be right up for it, but Liverpool have teed themselves up for a good performance at midday on Sunday.

Weird kick-off time, by the way.

Mauricio Pochettino, Man United boss, speaking to TNT Sports:.

In a recent development, here's the Alisson assist from earlier. Playmaker stuff from Liverpool's number one. Always thought he could have played outfield.

Manchester United just hate playing away in Europe.

United are now winless in their last seven Champions League away games (D3 L4).

It has been revealed that their worst-ever run is eight... which they could well match after playing their final away match in the league phase in January.

Villarreal are waiting for them.

Licensing mechanisms during RNA-guided DNA integration by type I-F3 CAST

📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 80 min read (16009 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nature

⏱️ ~80 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering.
  • A long-standing challenge in genome engineering is how to achieve precise, programmable integration of large (≥1 kb) DNA cargo.
  • R and L, right and left transposon ends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Precise genomic integration of large DNA cargo remains a central challenge in genome engineering. CRISPR-associated transposases (CASTs)1,2 offer a promising solution by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration. Because of their exceptional targeting fidelity, type I-F3 CASTs have been a major research focus1, yet the structural basis of their RNA-guided DNA integration has remained unclear. Here, using cryo-electron microscopy, computational protein design and functional assays, we report the licensing mechanisms that control DNA integration activity of Vibrio cholerae CAST (VchCAST). Structural determination was enabled by zero-shot computational redesign of TnsA, which enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude without compromising specificity. The structure of the holo integration complex reveals the conformational licensing events that govern activation of the integration machinery at the on-target site. Multiple components (Cascade–TniQ, TnsC and TnsA–TnsB) undergo conformational changes upon assembly into the holo integration complex, and the catalytically competent state is stabilized only within the full assembly. Comparison with existing CAST integration complex structures reveals conserved architectural features, suggesting a common molecular basis for RNA-guided transposition across CASTs. Our findings establish a general mechanistic framework for RNA-guided DNA integration and demonstrate that protein design is a powerful strategy for engineering highly active CAST systems.

A long-standing challenge in genome engineering is how to achieve precise, programmable integration of large (≥1 kb) DNA cargo. CRISPR–Cas nucleases are capable of efficient DNA cleavage3, but their reliance on host DNA repair pathways limits both the efficiency and fidelity of large insertions4. CASTs offer an alternative strategy by coupling RNA-guided DNA recognition to transposon-mediated integration, without the need for DNA double-strand breaks or homologous recombination1,2. CASTs evolved from Tn7-like transposons through the acquisition of a CRISPR effector, with distinct effectors defining each of the major subfamilies: type V-K, I-F3, I-B and I-D5. All CASTs encode a conserved set of proteins: TniQ (bridging protein), TnsC (AAA+ regulator) and TnsA–TnsB (TnsA/B, transposase complex) (Fig. 1a). The CRISPR effector and TniQ form the targeting module, and TnsA/B and TnsC form the transposition machinery (Fig. 1a). Although all CASTs perform RNA-guided transposition, they can display a remarkable diversity of targeting behaviours. For example, in type I-B2 CASTs, the transposition machinery can associate with either the sequence-specific DNA-binding protein TnsD or an RNA-guided targeting complex6. Type V-K CASTs exhibit a robust off-target pathway, driven by the propensity of TniQ and TnsC to load at non-cognate sites7. Type I-F3 CASTs have a Cascade effector and exhibit near-exclusive on-target integration8, which makes them of particular interest for clinical9 and microbial genome-editing applications10.

Recent structural studies of CAST assemblies have begun to reveal how this conserved transposition machinery accommodates architecturally diverse CRISPR effectors. The V-K system from Scytonema hofmannii, ShCAST, is the best characterized to date; its holo integration complex (HIC) structure demonstrates that the host factor S15 and TniQ associate with Cas12k and together strongly distort target DNA, an event that is required to recruit two helical turns of hexameric TnsC11,12, which in turn engages the transposase TnsB via its C-terminal hook13. A complete TnsABCD integration complex structure exists for type I-B2 CAST14, but structural information on other CAST assemblies is limited to isolated components or subcomplexes. TnsC organization is not fixed across CAST systems, as it forms a heptameric ring in other CAST systems, including I-F315 and I-B216, as well as in Tn717. Whether mechanistic insights from one system can be extended to other CAST systems is unclear.

Industry observers note that despite extensive biochemical, genetic and structural studies of individual components, the mechanisms by which type I-F3 CASTs achieve precise on-target integration remain unknown. Chromatin immunoprecipitation with sequencing (ChIP–seq) experiments have revealed a hierarchical assembly pathway in which Cascade–TniQ occupancy precedes TnsC recruitment, and stable TnsC accumulation depends on the transposase TnsA/B15. Cascade–TniQ binds DNA promiscuously and forms partial R-loops at many candidate sites15, but they cannot complete R-loop formation on their own18, suggesting that additional steps are required to license TnsC recruitment. Structures of TnsC15 have established the molecular details of its homo-oligomerization on DNA. Nonetheless, how all these components come together to form an integration-competent complex at the RNA-guided target site remains unknown. Thus, a structure of the fully assembled HIC is critical to establish the mechanistic basis for RNA-guided DNA integration and for rational engineering efforts to improve type I-F3 CAST integration efficiency for translational applications9,19.

It has been revealed that here, using a combination of computational protein design, single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) and directed in vivo mutagenesis, we uncover the mechanisms that regulate HIC assembly in the type I-F3 VchCAST system. The architectures of the strand-transfer complex (STC) and the full HIC reveal how RNA-guided target recognition, TnsC oligomerization and TnsA/B recruitment converge to organize a stable integration complex. Despite large structural differences across type V-K, I-F3 and I-B2 CASTs, conserved local features suggest universal mechanistic principles of RNA-guided DNA integration across CASTs. Our results reveal a context-dependent structural mechanism, whereby each of the aforementioned components undergoes significant conformational rearrangements relative to their isolated structures15,18,20 as a means to license RNA-guided integration complex assembly. Our work also demonstrates how structure-guided computational protein design can be leveraged as a highly effective strategy for improving integration activity without compromising specificity.

Industry observers note that because TnsA was refractory to purification (Methods), we hypothesized that stabilizing it in a product-bound conformation could both enhance activity and facilitate structure determination. We therefore modelled the VchCAST STC (comprising TnsA, TnsB and a strand-transfer DNA substrate) using AlphaFold 321 (Extended Data Fig. 1). We then redesigned the TnsA sequence using LigandMPNN22, with functionally important residues held fixed (32%; 74 out of 230 residues; Supplementary Fig. 1) and applied per-residue sampling biased towards TnsA homologues. Designs were grouped by sequence divergence from wild-type TnsA (TnsAWT), then selected for experimental screening on the basis of predicted confidence scores (Methods).

Industry observers note that we screened 500 top-ranking designs, each containing between 2 and 87 substitutions (Supplementary Table 1), using our previously developed high-throughput Escherichia coli screen23. In brief, a kanamycin resistance cassette serves as the donor DNA, such that kanamycin selection reports overall integration activity. On-target genomic integration is enriched by dual kanamycin and arabinose selection, which selects for disruption of an arabinose-inducible ccdB toxin gene. Activity and specificity scores are calculated as the log2-transformed fold change in variant frequency compared to wild type23. Of the 500 designs tested, 67% showed higher activity than TnsAWT (Fig. 1b). The top-performing design (D1A; Fig. 1b) incorporates 27 mutations (Extended Data Fig. 2) and has a log2-transformed activity score of 6.37, with no significant change in specificity (specificity score = −0.27; Fig. 1b). This improvement translates in vivo to an approximately 100-fold increase in integration activity relative to TnsAWT (Fig. 1c) while maintaining high fidelity, with 98% of insertions occurring on target (Fig. 1d) and at the expected distance, 82 base pairs (bp) from the protospacer adjacent motif (PAM)1 (Fig. 1e).

TnsA is required for transposition, but its catalytic activity determines product identity: cleavage of the 5′ donor end generates simple insertions, whereas a failure to cleave generates co-integrates24. Long-read sequencing distinguishes these two products, establishing the extent of TnsA activity8. Using long-read sequencing, we found that D1A produced more co-integrates than wild-type TnsA (42% simple insertions versus 96.2%; Extended Data Fig. 3). This phenotype was attributable primarily to the Q73K substitution: reverting Q73 to the wild-type residue restored simple insertion frequency to near wild-type levels (92.4%) without compromising the transposition activity gains conferred by the broader D1A redesign (Extended Data Fig. 3), indicating that Q73K governs the simple insertion/co-integrate balance independently of those gains. This also does not appear to be a general consequence of the design campaign, as other top-scoring designs retain full catalytic activity (97–100% simple insertions; Extended Data Fig. 3). Finally, we examined the effect of redesign on the folded state of TnsA. Circular dichroism analysis revealed that TnsAWT has substantial random coil content, consistent with an unfolded protein, whereas D1A has a spectrum consistent with a well-folded, mostly α-helical protein (Supplementary Fig. 2). Together, these results demonstrate that zero-shot structure-based computational design can both improve CAST activity and facilitate structure determination, creating a framework for iterative structure-guided optimization.

According to recent reports, we next determined the cryo-EM structure of the STC containing integration host factor (IHF), D1A (hereafter referred to as TnsA), TnsB and a strand-transfer DNA substrate (2.9 Å overall resolution; Fig. 1f,g and Supplementary Figs. 3 and 4). We found that K73 occupies a second-shell position relative to the TnsA active site, sufficiently close to form a hydrogen bond with catalytic residues, providing a likely explanation for why the Q73K substitution reduces the catalytic activity of TnsA (Supplementary Fig. 5). As this perturbation is confined to the local active site environment, the D1A structure presented here should therefore represent an otherwise catalytically competent state. IHF promotes CAST transposition 10-fold, although it is not absolutely required for activity25. In our structure, IHF binds LE DNA at a site between LE1 and LE2 (Supplementary Fig. 3), bending the DNA to permit occupancy of additional TnsB binding sites. This binding mode has been described in molecular detail in a related study that lacked TnsA and other components of the HIC20. Here, we instead focus on the novel insights we observe in the presence of the partner protein TnsA.

Industry observers note that tnsA localizes to the 5′ end of the donor DNA, where it binds the flanking host DNA and forms a continuous β-sheet with TnsB, a feature highly similar to previous TnsA structures from the type I-B2 PmcCAST system (Supplementary Fig. 6). We also identified conformational flexibility in the STC ensemble, which was separable by 3D classification. The highest-resolution class, containing the majority of particles, corresponds to class 1 (Supplementary Fig. 7a), whereas a second, minor 3D class (27% of particles, 3.2 Å overall resolution) lacks observable density for target DNA and for TnsB beyond the C-terminal helix (CTH) domain (class 2; Supplementary Fig. 7b,c and Extended Data Table 1). Closer inspection of class 2 reveals that the catalytic DDE triad (D223, D308, and E344) is too distant (6.2–6.9 Å; Supplementary Fig. 8) to form a functional active site, and that the loop preceding E344 (residues 331–341) is disordered (Fig. 1i). By contrast, class 1 has the expected arrangement of catalytic residues, as well as two magnesium ions: a catalytic magnesium with the expected coordination geometry and a second structural magnesium positioned nearby that stabilizes a sharp bend at the target–donor DNA junction (Fig. 1j). The conformational transition from class 2 to class 1 would entail a ~20° rotation of the catalytic domain and target DNA-binding domain (TBD) of TnsB at the TnsA–TnsB interface (blue star, Fig. 1h), reorienting these domains to engage target DNA. Concurrently, a target DNA-binding loop in the catalytic domain of TnsB (residues 359–378) becomes structured, further priming the complex for target DNA binding (Fig. 1k). These structural observations show that the STC exhibits conformational heterogeneity; one conformation (class 2) appearing catalytically inactive, and the other (class 1) showing rearrangements consistent with active site organization and target DNA engagement. As TnsA/B requires additional transposon-encoded partner proteins (that is, TnsC) for integration activity1, these conformational changes may reflect a mechanism of activation for TnsA/B.

Recent findings suggest that we next determined the cryo-EM structure of the HIC, comprising Cascade–TniQ, TnsA, TnsB and TnsC, assembled on a strand-transfer DNA substrate that mimics the in vivo integration product (Supplementary Fig. 3). Our cryo-EM data analysis reveals substantial compositional heterogeneity, with three identifiable assemblies (Extended Data Fig. 4): Cascade–TniQ (target-recognition complex (TRC); 3 Å overall resolution), STC–TnsC (4.3 Å overall resolution) and the HIC (4.5 Å overall resolution; Fig. 2a). In the HIC, local resolution is highest at the Cascade core (3.7 Å) and decreases towards the STC periphery (about 7 Å; Extended Data Table 1 and Supplementary Fig. 9). Although IHF was included in the reconstitution, we did not observe IHF bound in the resulting structure, which may be attributable to the sample preparation method (Methods). Notably, the overall map was of sufficient quality to interpret different structural features without the need of a composite map stitched from subtracted focused-refined regions.

It has been revealed that the HIC contains a Cascade effector, a TniQ dimer, a heptameric TnsC ring, a TnsB tetramer and two copies of TnsA (Fig. 2b), consistent with the stoichiometry established by structures of individual subcomplexes15,18,20. However, density for the seventh TnsC protomer (TnsC7) is noticeably weaker than for the other subunits (Supplementary Fig. 10), indicating substoichiometric occupancy or flexibility. The DNA-binding footprint accounts for the characteristic 82 bp integration distance from the PAM: 32 nucleotides occupied by the guide RNA spacer, followed by a 21, 14 and 15 bp footprint corresponding to TniQ, TnsC and TnsB, respectively, and terminating in a 5-nucleotide target-site duplication (Fig. 2c). Mutagenesis of the Cas8/5 PAM-interacting residues S127, R243, N246 and D461 substantially reduces integration activity (Supplementary Fig. 11), consistent with an notable role for these residues in PAM recognition and transposition. Our structure of the VchCAST HIC reveals an arrangement wherein TnsC acts as a bifunctional adaptor, interacting with TniQ via its N-terminal face and with the STC via its C-terminal face (Fig. 2b). This architectural role of TnsC is similar to previous observations in ShCAST (type V-K)12 and PmcCAST (type I-B2) systems14,16. This modularity explains how CAST systems have diversified to co-opt a wide range of CRISPR effectors while preserving the core transposition mechanism.

Sources indicate that A central question is how the targeting module is physically coupled to the core transposition machinery. In the HIC, TniQ2 serves as the primary physical bridge between the target recognition and transposition machinery (Fig. 3a), forming a predominantly hydrophobic interface with TnsC1 (Fig. 3b). Consistent with the functional importance of this interface, alanine substitutions at F2, L3 and F40 substantially reduced integration activity (Fig. 3c). TniQ forms a constitutive homodimer, but only the TniQ2 monomer interacts with TnsC, mirroring observations in the evolutionarily distant ShCAST and PmcCAST, in which a single TniQ subunit recruits TnsC12,16. Remarkably, despite the divergent overall architectures of the ShCAST (Protein Data Bank (PDB): 8EA3), PmcCAST (PDB: 8FF4) and VchCAST integration complexes, the TniQ–TnsC interface is notably conserved (Extended Data Fig. 5). In particular, the TnsC finger loop, previously shown to mediate critical TniQ interactions in ShCAST12, engages TniQ2 similarly in VchCAST (Extended Data Fig. 5). Consistent with this observation, truncations within the TnsC finger loop severely reduce transposition activity15. These findings identify the TniQ–TnsC interface as a shared docking point that may enable architecturally diverse CRISPR effectors to couple to common transposition machinery.

Recent findings suggest that tnsB activity is strictly dependent on TnsC-mediated recruitment to the target site15, making these interactions central to understanding integration. We next examined how TnsB engages TnsC within the HIC, revealing multiple points of contact along the C-terminal face of TnsC, specifically at protomers TnsC2, TnsC3 and TnsC6 (Fig. 3d). Notably, the TBD of TnsB localizes to the TnsC2–TnsC3 interface (Fig. 3e), consistent with previous ShCAST and PmcCAST structures12,14 (Extended Data Fig. 6). Across Tn7-like transposons, ATP binding, but not hydrolysis, is required for integration activity26,27. AAA+ initiator clade regulators require ATP for oligomerization, as the ATP-binding pocket is formed at the inter-protomer interface28. This implies that transposition requires TnsC oligomerization on target DNA, although the mechanistic basis for this requirement has remained unclear. The conserved interaction between the TBD of TnsB and the TnsC inter-protomer interface now suggests that TnsB directly senses the oligomeric state of TnsC, providing a structural explanation for this long-standing observation.

It has been revealed that another conserved feature across CAST systems is the interaction between TnsC and the extreme C terminus of TnsB, known as the hook, which is critical for transposition13. The interchangeability of TnsB hooks between type I-F3 CASTs29 underscores the importance of these structured interactions within otherwise disordered regions. Consistent with this role, we observe continuous density connecting the CTH (residues 563–573) of TnsB to the surface of TnsC6 (Fig. 3f), although additional contacts are likely to remain undetected owing to the length and extensive disorder of this region. The TnsB hook is predicted by AlphaFold 321 to correspond to the last eight residues of TnsB, an assignment supported by cryo-EM density observed in the HIC (Extended Data Fig. 7). The hook binding site in VchTnsC aligns well with ShTnsC13 and PmcTnsC14 (Extended Data Fig. 7), indicating that although structural details may differ, the binding location is conserved.

It has been revealed that having identified the TnsB hook interaction with TnsC, we reasoned that the disordered N- and C-terminal regions in all components of the core transposition machinery (TnsABC; Supplementary Fig. 12) could mediate additional interactions. Consistent with this idea, we observed contacts between the N terminus of TnsB and TnsA, and between the C-terminal tail of TnsC and TnsB (Fig. 3g). Residues 3–10 of the disordered N terminus of TnsB occupy a hydrophobic pocket on TnsA (Fig. 3h) close to aromatic residues F6 and F9, consistent with AlphaFold 3 predictions21 (Extended Data Fig. 1) and sequence conservation analysis (Extended Data Fig. 8a). Although N-terminal truncation (Δ1–10) caused a significant reduction in transposition activity, the TnsB F9A mutation reproduced almost none of this effect, suggesting that residues other than F9 mediate the relevant contacts within the truncated region (Extended Data Fig. 8c). The C-terminal tail of TnsC (residues 321–330) is positioned against the CTH of TnsB (Fig. 3i and Extended Data Fig. 8b) at a hydrophobic interface, also supported by AlphaFold 3 predictions21 (Supplementary Fig. 13) and conservation analysis (Extended Data Fig. 8b). The TnsC F329A mutation almost fully abrogated transposition activity, similar to the effect of C-terminal truncation of TnsC (Extended Data Fig. 8c). Analogous interactions between the C terminus of TnsC and the STC occur in PmcCAST, albeit involving different subunits and interfaces14 (Extended Data Fig. 9). These findings uncover a previously unrecognized network of interactions involving the unstructured termini of TnsA, TnsB and TnsC, revealing how the core transposition machinery may maintain associations to facilitate integration-competent assembly.

Recent findings suggest that A previous cryo-EM structure of VchTnsC solved in the presence of DNA revealed an open heptameric ring-like arrangement in which the bound DNA was poorly resolved (PDB: 7UFI)15. In our HIC structure, although we clearly resolved the path of target DNA, no specific TnsC–DNA interactions could be precisely mapped. Thus, it is likely that the TnsC ring primarily associates with target DNA via the complementary basic surface formed by its central pore (Supplementary Fig. 14). This is consistent with previous data showing that TnsC binds DNA relatively weakly15, suggesting that TnsC requires partner proteins such as TniQ to initiate oligomerization on target DNA. Notably, comparison with PDB 7UFI reveals that the heptameric ring is significantly more open in the HIC. Aligning on TnsC1 results in an 11 Å displacement at TnsC7 relative to the equivalent protomer in PDB 7UFI (Fig. 3j), the result of an average 0.8 Å greater rise per protomer (Supplementary Fig. 15). This indicates that partner proteins induce larger conformational changes than those observed in TnsC with DNA alone. Our observations suggest that the oligomeric state of TnsC is sensitive to the presence of the partner proteins TniQ and TnsB and is mediated through distinct interaction interfaces located on specific TnsC protomers.

We next investigated how TnsC is selectively recruited to the target site. The compositional heterogeneity of our reconstitution enabled us to resolve a free Cascade–TniQ complex (Extended Data Fig. 4) (TRC; 3.0 Å overall resolution; Fig. 4a) that closely resembles a prior structure of the target DNA-bound VchCAST Cascade–TniQ complex18 (Supplementary Fig. 16). This previously reported structure featured a partial R-loop and a disordered Cas8/5 helical bundle domain (HBD)18. By contrast, the Cascade–TniQ complex in the HIC (Fig. 4b) adopts a fully engaged conformation characterized by a complete R-loop and a structured Cas8/5 HBD. Comparison of Cascade–TniQ in the TRC and HIC structures reveals that R-loop completion is accompanied by a conformational change in TniQ2 to engage both target DNA and TnsC (Extended Data Fig. 10).

Recent findings suggest that the non-target genomic strand (NTGS) is threaded through an electropositive channel at the tripartite TniQ1–TniQ2–Cas8/5 HBD interface, where it rejoins the target genomic strand (TGS) to reform the target DNA duplex downstream of the R-loop junction (Fig. 4c,d). The Cas8/5 HBD contributes to this channel through electrostatic contacts with the NTGS via R310, R311, K314 and R370 (Supplementary Fig. 17). Additionally, a previously uncharacterized loop within the Cas8/5 HBD (residues KSLIPEN), which we term the TniQ-interacting loop (TIL), interacts directly with TniQ1 (Fig. 4e). The functional importance of this interface is confirmed by alanine substitutions in the Cas8/5 HBD, TIL and at TniQ1 residues D361, S358 and W394, all of which substantially reduce integration activity (Figs. 3c and 4f).

According to recent reports, separately, TniQ2 engages target DNA through two distinct modes: hydrophobic packing against the R-loop junction (L326, L336, V362 and T363; Fig. 4g) and electrostatic interactions with the DNA backbone via basic and polar residues (R58, K65, R71, S104 and S106; Fig. 4h,i). Mutagenesis of residues at both interfaces substantially reduces integration activity, consistent with their functional importance (Fig. 3c). These observations establish that R-loop completion drives a conformational transition in the target recognition module that repositions TniQ to engage target DNA and license recruitment of the core transposition machinery.

Recent findings suggest that we propose the following working model for RNA-guided transposition, based on our findings and incorporating prior observations on CASTs and other Tn7-like systems. Cascade–TniQ promiscuously samples genomic locations15, consistent with its ability to stably bind target DNA with only partial R-loop formation (Fig. 5). A cooperative conformational rearrangement in Cas8/5 and TniQ is required to stabilize the full R-loop and enable TnsC recruitment, with direct contacts of TniQ at the R-loop junction providing a structural readout of R-loop completion. This coupling is further supported by molecular dynamics simulations demonstrating correlated motions between Cas8/5 and TniQ30. We observe no other DNA distortions consistent with specific recognition of the target site by the transposon-encoded machinery (Supplementary Fig. 18), contrary to that observed in other Tn7-like systems14,31. Further insight into target-site selectivity comes from the observation that PAM-distal mismatches permit Cascade binding but abolish transposition15. The conformational rearrangements in the HIC occur near spacer nucleotide positions 25–32, raising the possibility that mismatches in this region could introduce geometric incompatibility that prevents stable docking of the HBD and subsequent TnsC recruitment (Fig. 5). TnsC oligomerization is required to recruit TnsA/B to the target site and may be sensed directly by TnsB through conserved interactions spanning TnsC protomers. Whether full heptamer formation is required prior to TnsA/B recruitment remains unknown and is not resolvable using our reconstitution approach; however, previous work on Tn7 suggests that oligomerization is completed prior to TnsA/B recruitment32.

Sources indicate that major licensing events during RNA-guided DNA integration directly at the CRISPR effector (a) and at the transposase (b). a, Top left, the TRC (PDB: 36BQ) displays an unstructured Cas8/5 helical bundle domain, a partial R-loop and an outward-open TniQ conformation. Unstructured regions are indicated with dotted lines. This state can sample many genomic locations (dotted arrows) in addition to the programmed target site (red box). Top right, upon recognition of the target, the TRC forms stabilizing interactions between Cas8/5 and TniQ, promoting R-loop completion and enabling recruitment of TnsC to complete this licensing step (lock symbol). Middle, off-target complexes (grey) are unable to form a complete R-loop (red X) and the Cas8/5 helical bundle domain remains flexible, and TnsC cannot be recruited. b, Top left, the TnsB-only STC (PDB: 9Y7B) contains flexible target-binding domains and an incompletely arranged active site, shown inside the white circle as a disconnected DDE catalytic triad. Top right and middle, upon addition of TnsA, the TnsA/B STC adopts two conformational states that exist in equilibrium: class 2 (PDB: 36BP) and class 1 (PDB: 36BO). The class 1 state exhibits the catalytically competent arrangement of the DDE triad (triangle within the circle). Dotted lines indicate flexible connections between components, including the interface between TnsA and TnsB. The targeting module (orange) and transposition module (purple) assemble with TnsC to form the HIC (PDB: 36AU). Both the targeting and the transposition modules adopt stable conformations and are locked into an integration-competent conformation. The DDE triad forms a catalytically competent active site. The C-terminal tails of TnsB and TnsC function to loosely couple components, with the hook of TnsB inserting into a TnsC pocket, forming β-sheet interactions (purple arrow), while the TnsC C-terminal tail contacts TnsB near target DNA. Dotted lines indicate disordered regions.

TnsB also undergoes multiple layers of activation through association with partner proteins TnsA and TnsC. In isolation, the DDE catalytic triad is improperly arranged and too distant to coordinate magnesium ion binding, and target DNA remains disordered even when a strand-transfer substrate is provided20. Association with TnsA is insufficient to fully stabilize the catalytically competent conformation (Fig. 5). Only in the context of the HIC, in which both TnsA and TnsC are present, are the catalytic residues locked into an integration-competent state and target DNA stably accommodated. Although our reliance on a strand-transfer substrate does not allow us to establish the stepwise order of these conformations directly, the inactive-to-active transition that we observe is, to our knowledge, unreported in CAST systems despite extensive structural work from our group and others13,14,33. Notably, a conceptually related precedent exists in IS21, where the transposase IstA transitions from an inactive to an active conformation upon association with its obligate AAA+ partner IstB34, suggesting that conformational licensing may be an effective mechanism for ensuring selective activation of integration across Tn7 and related transposons. In summary, we propose that each component of the integration machinery undergoes conformational changes upon incorporation into the HIC, providing a structural basis for the exceptionally high on-target specificity characteristic of type I-F3 CAST systems. Both the targeting module Cascade–TniQ and the transposase TnsA/B serve to license RNA-guided DNA integration, ensuring that catalytic competence is only achieved upon assembly of the complete machinery at the RNA-guided target site.

Industry observers note that structured interactions embedded within intrinsically disordered regions of CAST proteins have critical roles in transposition, most notably through the C-terminal hook of TnsB12,29. Here, combining our cryo-EM structure with AlphaFold 3 predictions, we localize the C-terminal hook of TnsB and identify its binding site on TnsC. We also identify two previously unrecognized interactions: the N terminus of TnsB engages a pocket on TnsA, and the C terminus of TnsC contacts TnsB in close proximity to target DNA. These findings reveal an extensive network of structured interactions within otherwise disordered termini that physically connect the core transposition machinery prior to integration complex assembly. The mapping of these contacts has direct implications for the rational engineering of chimeric CAST systems and the design of improved variants.

The structural characterization of CAST systems has been largely motivated by the goal of engineering more efficient tools for genome editing; however, structure-guided efforts to improve CAST activity have had limited success29,35,36. Here we demonstrate that a high-throughput structure-based design approach can overcome these limitations, presenting a compelling and scalable alternative to directed evolution. We propose that thermodynamic stabilization of the integration-competent conformation is key to improve activity. This is consistent with the thermodynamic requirements of cut-and-paste transposition: the chemically isoenergetic reaction proceeds through states of increasing stability, and the product complex can be so stable that unfoldases (for example, ClpX) are required for its disassembly in vivo37. Consistent with this hypothesis, zero-shot structure-based protein design of a single protein, TnsA, enhanced integration activity by nearly two orders of magnitude in E. coli, approaching the gains achieved through seven rounds of directed evolution applied across the entire PseCAST system19. Notably, the redesigned variant not only improved integration activity but also enabled structural characterization of the HIC, illustrating how computational design and structural biology can be synergistic approaches.

According to recent reports, the compromised catalytic activity of the top design variant D1A is attributable primarily to a lysine substitution at position 73, which is within range to form hydrogen-bonding interactions with the catalytic residue D91. We hypothesized that this substitution directly perturbs active site chemistry, which motivated our prioritization of the reversion mutant for testing; consistent with this hypothesis, reversion almost fully restored catalytic activity while maintaining substantial increases in activity. This trade-off reflects a known limitation of structure-based design methods: approaches such as ProteinMPNN can inadvertently stabilize protein structure at the expense of catalytic function38, as functional residues are often locally destabilizing to the protein fold39. Therefore, success of the design strategy proposed here depends on mechanistic knowledge and the availability of a high-quality model of the integration-competent complex, precisely what the structures presented here provide, and what has been lacking in previous engineering efforts.

The codon-optimized gene encoding VchTnsB from V. cholerae Tn6677 was subcloned into the pARZ4 expression vector carrying a carbenicillin resistance marker, which was engineered to append an N-terminal hexahistidine (His6) tag followed by a maltose-binding protein (MBP) tag and a TEV protease recognition site. The sequence-verified construct was introduced into One Shot BL21(DE3) chemically competent E. coli cells (Invitrogen) for recombinant production.

According to recent reports, expression cultures were grown in 2× YT medium supplemented with 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin at 37 °C with shaking until OD600 reached 0.4–0.6. Cells were collected by centrifugation at 5,000 rpm for 20 min at 4 °C and resuspended in lysis buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 8.0), 500 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA, 0.1% NP-40, 1 mM DTT, and protease inhibitor cocktail (Thermo Fisher Scientific; one tablet per 30 ml). Cells were lysed by probe sonication on ice using alternating 5 s on–10 s off cycles, and insoluble debris was removed by centrifugation at 16,000 rpm for 30 min at 4 °C.

Peak fractions were pooled and diluted to 200 mM NaCl using heparin dilution buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.4, 50 mM NaCl, 5% glycerol) before loading onto a HiTrap Heparin HP column (Cytiva) on an ÄKTA Pure FPLC system. In vivo transposition assays were performed in E. coli cJP003 recipient cells, which carry an arabinose-inducible ccdB toxin cassette integrated at the intended genomic target site23. Two compatible pHelpers were co-transformed into the recipient strain: one encoding the VchCAST transposition machinery (TnsB, TnsC and either TnsA or D1A) with carbenicillin resistance (adapted from Addgene #130633), and a second encoding the VchCAST targeting machinery (TniQ, Cas8/5, Cas7, Cas6 and ccdB-targeting single guide RNA (sgRNA)) with chloramphenicol resistance (adapted from Addgene #130635). For the assays of mutants, point mutations were introduced into pHelpers by site-directed mutagenesis using KLD Enzyme Mix (NEB, M0554S). Primers used for mutagenesis are listed in Supplementary Table 2.

Freshly transformed cells were first grown in 5 ml LB medium, inoculated into 50 ml LB medium containing carbenicillin, chloramphenicol, and 0.1 mM IPTG. Cultures were grown at 37 °C with shaking until the OD600 reached 0.6–0.8. Cells were collected, washed 3 times with ice-cold 10% glycerol, and normalized to equivalent cell densities. Recipient cells were electroporated with a non-replicating VchCAST pDonor carrying an R6K origin of replication at 5:1 plasmid-to-cell ratio. Cells were immediately resuspended in 1 ml SOC medium, recovered at 37 °C with shaking for 1 h, and incubated overnight at 30 °C without shaking to promote transposition. Cells were then diluted to obtain countable colonies and plated on LB agar plates containing 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol, with or without 0.1% (w/v) l-arabinose to assess overall activity (kanamycin) or on-target activity (kanamycin plus arabinose), respectively.

Industry observers note that A structural model of the TnsA/B STC with target and donor DNA was generated using AlphaFold 321 and used as input for structure-based sequence design. Protein and DNA substrate sequences are provided in Supplementary Table 3.

The AlphaFold 3-generated TnsA–TnsB STC model was used as input for structure-based protein design. A total of 74 TnsA residue positions were fixed during design based on five structural criteria: (1) residues predicted to participate in primary or secondary interactions with the active site; (2) residues within contact distance of the DNA; (3) residues predicted to form protein–protein interfaces with TnsB; (4) residues predicted to contribute to a binding pocket engaging the TnsB or TnsC hook regions; and (5) N- and C-terminal residues with low predicted confidence (pLDDT), indicative of structural disorder. The full set of designable positions is listed in Supplementary Table 4.

Recent findings suggest that sequences were generated using three graph neural network-based protein design methods that sample amino acid probabilities from local structural context: LigandMPNN22, SolubleMPNN40 and HyperMPNN41. Because these models are trained on structural rather than functional information, and because design was performed on an AlphaFold 3 model rather than an experimentally determined structure, a bias towards TnsA sequences was introduced to restrict sampling to structurally favourable substitutions and improve the likelihood of recovering functional variants. Bias was applied by modifying per-residue logits prior to softmax normalization, such that increasing bias values progressively shifted the amino acid probability distribution towards the native identity without fully enforcing it. Bias strengths of 0, 1, 2, 3 and 4 were applied to each of the three models using the flag bias_AA_per_residue. In a parallel strategy, an additional sampling bias was introduced towards residues conserved in a multiple sequence alignment of TnsA homologues.

Industry observers note that all designed sequences were folded as monomers and as part of the STC using Chai-142. Designed sequences were clustered using MMseqs243, and final designs were selected from each strategy based on threshold criteria across six metrics: backbone root mean square deviation (RMSD) of monomeric TnsA relative to input structure (<0.9–1.2 Å, depending on design strategy), backbone RMSD of predicted STC complex (<1.5–1.7 Å), predicted TM-score of the monomer (>0.918–0.928), predicted interface TM-score of the STC (>0.839–0.845), predicted local distance difference test (pLDDT) of the monomer (>0.893–0.910), and pLDDT of the STC (>0.834–0.840).

According to recent reports, in total, 499 designed TnsA variants were selected for experimental screening. One additional sequence was independently generated using PROSS44, yielding a final library of 500 sequences (Supplementary Table 1).

A TnsA entry vector was constructed by replacing the TnsAWT region of the VchCAST TnsABC pHelper (Addgene #130633) with BsaI flanking sites. Nucleotide sequences of TnsA designs (693 bp) were fragmented into 300 bp oligonucleotides containing BsaI flanking sites, unique primer-binding sites, and unique per-design barcodes using the OMEGA program45 and purchased from Twist Bioscience. The oligonucleotide pools were PCR-amplified and inserted into the entry vector by Golden Gate assembly at a 20:1 insert-to-vector molar ratio. The assembled TnsA library was purified and electroporated into NEB 10-beta electrocompetent E. coli (NEB, #C3020K). Cells were plated on agar plates containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin after 1 h recovery at 37 °C. Colonies were collected at greater than 100× coverage per variant to ensure adequate library representation, and the TnsA library plasmid pool was extracted using the ZymoPURE II Plasmid Midiprep Kit (Zymo Research, D4201).

cJP003 cells were transformed with a Cascade–TniQ pHelper plasmid encoding TniQ, Cascade, a ccdB-targeting guide RNA, and a chloramphenicol resistance marker. Transformed cells were rendered electrocompetent by three successive washes with ice-cold 10% glycerol. The TnsA library was electroporated into the prepared cells at a 0.5:1 plasmid-to-cell ratio to ensure that each cell received a unique TnsABC pHelper variant. Cells were recovered at 37 °C for 1 h and plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol. Colonies were collected at greater than 100× coverage per variant and cultured at 37 °C in LB medium supplemented with 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol.

Upon reaching OD600 ≈ 0.6, cells were collected and washed 3 times with 10% glycerol to prepare electrocompetent recipient cells. At this step, pHelper plasmids from a subset of recipient cells were extracted as input reference samples using the Monarch Spin Plasmid Miniprep Kit (NEB, T1110L). Recipient cells were electroporated with the non-replicable VchCAST pDonor at a 5:1 plasmid-to-cell ratio, immediately resuspended in 1 ml SOC medium, and recovered at 37 °C with shaking for 1 h. Cells were subsequently incubated overnight at 30 °C without shaking. The following day, cells were plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol for the activity screen, or on the same agar additionally supplemented with 0.1% (w/v) L-arabinose for the specificity screen. pHelper plasmids were extracted from selected colonies collected at greater than 100× coverage per variant using the ZymoPURE II Plasmid Midiprep Kit. All steps were performed in biological duplicate.

Barcode regions from the input reference and screened plasmid pools were PCR-amplified and indexed using the Nextera XT Index Kit v2 Set A (Illumina, FC-131-2001). Primers used for NGS are provided in Supplementary Table 5. Indexed amplicons were sequenced on an in-house MiSeq instrument. Activity and specificity scores for each design were calculated using an Enrich2-based pipeline23,46 on a log2-fold change basis and normalized to the score of TnsAWT.

E. coli cells that had undergone in vivo transposition assays were plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin and 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol to select for all integration events. More than 1,000 colonies were scraped for gDNA extraction using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (Promega, A1125). Tagmentation-based transposon insertion sequencing (TagTn-seq)11 was performed on the extracted gDNA. Libraries were prepared by fragmenting gDNA with the Nextera XT DNA Library Kit (Illumina, FC-131-1024), followed by PCR amplification using an i7 primer and VchCAST right-end (RE)-specific primers, and indexing prior to sequencing on the in-house MiSeq. Reads mapping to the intact VchCAST pDonor were filtered from the resulting sequencing data using BBMap (v39.80), and RE-adjacent sequences were mapped to the cJP003 genome to profile integration site distribution.

TnsA activity is assessed through the formation of simple insertion products, as TnsA-mediated DNA cleavage results in cleavage of the 5′ end of donor DNA and lack of cleavage results in integration of the donor DNA backbone, otherwise referred to as co-integrates. We used long-read sequencing to distinguish between these two products, as previously established8.

Recent findings suggest that E. coli cells that had undergone in vivo transposition assays were plated on agar containing 100 µg ml−1 carbenicillin, 50 µg ml−1 kanamycin, 30 µg ml−1 chloramphenicol, and 0.1% (w/v) l-arabinose to select specifically for on-target integration events. More than 1,000 colonies were scraped and gDNA was extracted using the Wizard Genomic DNA Purification Kit (ProMega, A1125). Whole-genome sequencing was performed by Plasmidsaurus. Sequencing reads were analysed to identify integration products by detecting reads containing both target-site and left-end (LE) sequences, which define the boundaries of the integrated region. Reads containing pDonor backbone sequence were classified as co-integrates, while reads lacking pDonor backbone but containing the downstream target-site sequence were classified as simple insertions. Reads lacking both features were classified as ambiguous.

Industry observers note that far-UV circular dichroism spectra were collected using a JASCO CD spectropolarimeter. WT-TnsA and D1A were buffer exchanged into 10 mM potassium phosphate (pH 7.4) and analysed at a final concentration of 15 µM using a 0.1 cm path length quartz cuvette. Spectra were recorded from 195 to 280 nm at room temperature in continuous scanning mode with a 1.0 nm bandwidth and a scan speed of 200 nm min−1. Eight accumulations were collected for each sample and averaged to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. A buffer-only spectrum was recorded under identical conditions and subtracted from each protein spectrum.

The corrected circular dichroism signal was converted to mean residue ellipticity according to the manufacturer’s instructions:.

where θobs is the buffer-subtracted ellipticity, n is the number of amino acid residues, c is the protein concentration (M), and l is the cuvette path length (cm). WT-TnsA and D1A were normalized using 229 and 236 amino acid residues, respectively. For plotting, mean residue ellipticity values were divided by 1,000 and are reported as [θ] ×10−3 (deg cm2 dmol−1).

The DNA substrate used was designed based on in vivo genomic profiling experiments, synthesized as single-stranded DNA, and annealed to form a strand-transfer product substrate which was used for complex reconstitution, following our previously described strategy12,13. The left end spans LE1 through LE3 (positions 1–109) and the right end spans RE1 through RE3 (1–72), as shown in Supplementary Fig. 4. The native arrangement of left and right ends are identical up to position 30 (encompassing the 8 bp terminal sequence and LE1/ RE1). Past the first binding site, the placement and spacing of LE2–LE3 and RE2–RE3 differ, additionally there is a IHF binding site between LE1 and LE2 (Supplementary Fig. 4).

Industry observers note that two double-stranded DNA substrates were independently assembled for the STC and transpososome reconstitution: a LE fragment and a RE fragment, each designed to recapitulate the relevant structural elements of the VchCAST RNA-guided transposition product, including the transposon terminal repeat sequences, the 5 bp target site duplication, and flanking target and gDNA regions (Supplementary Table 6). A diagram of the substrates can be found in Supplementary Fig. 4.

The LE fragment was assembled from three oligonucleotides: LE–TGS, which contains the transposon LE and flanking gDNA, Target-RC, which completes the double-stranded target genomic region, and LE–HFR, which provides the complementary LE region to LE–TGS along with a host flanking region for TnsA binding.

The RE fragment was assembled from four oligonucleotides: RE–TGS, which contains the RE and the target strand for guide RNA binding, NTGS–Scramble, a non-target strand oligonucleotide contained a scrambled sequence to facilitate bubble formation, RE–HFR, an oligonucleotide that complements the RE sequence of RE–TGS and contains a flanking HFR region, and DTB–LUEGO, a desthiobiotinylated oligonucleotide incorporated at the 5′ end of the RE fragment to enable streptavidin-based affinity capture of the assembled complexes during pull-down experiments47.

Prior to annealing, all oligonucleotides were purified by HPLC using an Agilent 1260 Infinity II system equipped with an AdvanceBio Oligonucleotide column (Agilent Technologies) to ensure incorporation of only full-length species. The LE and RE fragments were each assembled independently by combining their respective oligonucleotides at equimolar concentrations in annealing buffer (10 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 50 mM NaCl, 1 mM EDTA), heating to 95 °C for 5 min, and gradually cooling to 50 °C at 1 °C per min using a thermal cycler (Bio-Rad). The annealed fragments were stored separately until used in STC and transpososome reconstitutions.

STC assembly reactions were prepared using an annealed DNA substrate (0.5 µM in 100 µl) and containing TnsB together with D1A using the same 1:5:10 stoichiometry. Complex assembly was initially carried out under high-salt conditions in a buffer containing 26 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 5 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 20 mM KCl, 750 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM MgCl2, 15 mM magnesium acetate, 2% glycerol, 1 mM DTT and 0.1% Tween-20. Following assembly, samples were dialysed overnight at 4 °C from high-salt buffer into an identical low-salt buffer in which the NaCl concentration was reduced to 150 mM to promote stable complex formation.

Recent findings suggest that for affinity capture of assembled complexes, Streptavidin Mag Sepharose magnetic beads (Cytiva) were washed 3 times with 500 μl of low-salt buffer prior to use. Dialysed samples were incubated with the equilibrated streptavidin beads for 1 h at room temperature with continuous rotation to allow binding of biotinylated DNA substrates and associated protein complexes.

It has been revealed that following incubation, the beads were washed 3 times with 500 μl of low-salt buffer to remove unbound proteins and nonspecific material. Bound complexes were subsequently eluted using low-salt buffer supplemented with 10 mM biotin. Elution was performed in 2 sequential rounds using 50 µl buffer per step, with each incubation carried out for 30 min at room temperature under rotation before collection of the eluate. Elution fractions were analysed by SDS–PAGE to confirm the presence of protein components within the assembled complexes. Sample quality, homogeneity and the presence of assembled STCs were further evaluated by negative-stain electron microscopy prior to cryo-EM grid preparation and vitrification.

Sequential on-bead assembly of the HIC was performed by first capturing the desthiobiotinylated RE substrate (0.5 µM in 100 µl) on Streptavidin Mag Sepharose magnetic beads (Cytiva). Binding was carried out for 1 h at room temperature with gentle rotation in binding buffer comprising 26 mM HEPES (pH 7.5), 5 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 20 mM KCl, 750 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM MgCl2, 15 mM MgOAc, 2% glycerol, 1 mM ATP, 1 mM DTT, and 0.1% Tween-20, followed by 3 washes with 500 µl of the same buffer.

Cascade–TniQ was subsequently introduced at a 1:2 DNA:protein molar ratio and incubated for 1 h at room temperature, followed by 3 washes. The LE substrate (0.5 µM), pre-complexed with E. coli IHF at a 1:8 DNA-to-protein molar ratio, was then added alongside TnsB (1:5 DNA:protein) and designed TnsA (1:10 DNA:protein), and the assembly was allowed to proceed for 1 h at room temperature. Beads were washed 3 times with 500 µl binding buffer. In the final step, TnsC was introduced at a 1:10 DNA-to-protein ratio in binding buffer supplemented with equimolar concentrations of ATP and ATPγS (1 mM each) and incubated for 1 h at room temperature. Unbound proteins were removed by 3 washes with 500 µl of ATP/ATPγS-containing binding buffer.

The assembled HIC was released from the beads by two sequential elution steps, each using 50 µl of elution buffer (binding buffer supplemented with 10 mM biotin) incubated under rotation for 30 min. Eluted fractions were resolved by SDS–PAGE to verify the presence of all HIC components. Prior to cryo-EM grid preparation, samples were evaluated by negative-stain electron microscopy to confirm the presence of assembled HIC particles and to assess sample homogeneity.

Sources indicate that graphene sheets with a poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) support layer (ACS Material, TTG100BB,25 ×25 mm) were stored at 4 °C until use. Graphene transfer onto cryo-EM grids was performed based on a previously described protocol with minor modifications48. Ultrafoil grids (Au R1.2/1.3, Quantifoil) were placed on a 3D-printed grid transfer tool immersed in deionized water. Excess support material from the graphene pad was trimmed, and the PMMA/graphene pad was placed gently onto the water surface to avoid overflow onto the graphene layer. After positioning, the water level was gradually lowered by syringe withdrawal, allowing the graphene sheet to settle onto the grids. Grids were left overnight at room temperature to anneal, then baked at 150 °C for 30 min to promote firm adhesion. Grids were transferred to a Petri dish, and PMMA was removed by three successive acetone washes. Graphene-coated grids were individually transferred to a grid box and stored at room temperature until use.

STC samples were prepared for cryo-EM either directly from pull-down elution fractions or following two- to four-fold dilution in low-salt buffer. Graphene-coated grids were prepared as described above. Prior to sample application, grids were plasma-cleaned using a Solarus II Plasma Cleaner (Gatan) under an Ar/O2 atmosphere at 10 W for 10 s (s), with the graphene-coated surface oriented upward.

For vitrification, 4 µl of STC sample was applied to the carbon side of a graphene-coated grid and incubated for 60 s inside a Vitrobot Mark IV chamber (Thermo Fisher Scientific) maintained at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity. Grids were blotted for 3.5 s at a blot force of −7 and immediately plunge-frozen into liquid ethane cooled by liquid nitrogen.

HIC samples were prepared for cryo-EM from either undiluted pull-down eluates or two- to four-fold dilutions thereof. Graphene-coated grids were prepared as described above and plasma-cleaned using a Solarus II Plasma Cleaner (Gatan) under an Ar/O2 atmosphere at 10 W for 10 s with the graphene-coated face oriented upward.

For vitrification, 4 µl of HIC sample was applied to the carbon side of a graphene-coated grid and incubated for 60 s inside a Vitrobot Mark IV chamber at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity. Grids were blotted for 3.5 s at a blot force of −7 before plunge-freezing into liquid ethane cooled by liquid nitrogen.

In a recent development, ni-NTA affinity grids were prepared as previously described49. Quantifoil Au R1.2/1.3 grids were coated with a Ni-NTA lipid monolayer composed of 20% 18:1 DGS-NTA(Ni) (Avanti Polar Lipids) diluted with DOPC (18:1; Avanti Polar Lipids). Grids were incubated with 3 µl of His-tagged HIC diluted in 2 µl of elution buffer (26 mM HEPES pH 7.5, 5 mM Tris-HCl pH 7.5, 20 mM KCl, 750 mM NaCl, 0.2 mM MgCl2, 15 mM MgOAc, 2% glycerol, 1 mM ATP, 1 mM DTT, 0.1% Tween-20) for 1 h at 4 °C in a humidity chamber to allow affinity capture. Unbound material was removed by three brief washes with elution buffer, after which grids were blotted and plunge-frozen in liquid ethane using a Vitrobot operated at 4 °C and 100% relative humidity with a blot force of −7 and blot time of 3.5 s.

Vitrified STC samples were initially screened on a Talos Arctica transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated with fringe-free illumination at 130,000× magnification (0.63 Å per pixel) and 200 kV, equipped with a Gatan K3 direct electron detector and a BioQuantum imaging filter (20 eV slit width). Data were collected using the EPU software package (Thermo Fisher Scientific). This screening step was used to assess grid quality and particle distribution prior to large-scale data collection. Grids of sufficient quality were subsequently imaged on a Titan Krios G3i transmission electron microscope (Thermo Fisher Scientific) operated with fringe-free illumination at 130,000× magnification (0.745 Å per pixel) and 300 kV, equipped with a Falcon 4i (4k × 4k) direct electron detector, a BioQuantum imaging filter, and a 20 eV energy-selecting slit. Data collection employed the aberration-free image shift and multi-shot-per-hole acquisition modes of EPU. For the STC dataset, 7,724 movies were collected using EPU with image shift, with nominal defocus ranging from −1.5 to −2.5 µm at 0.2 µm intervals. Each movie was acquired with a 3.1 s exposure and a total dose of 60 e− Å−2, fractionated into 60 frames. Frames were aligned using MotionCor250, and CTF estimation was performed in cryoSPARC v4.7.151. The full data processing workflow is presented in Supplementary Fig. 4.

Recent findings suggest that particles were initially picked using blob picker, and approximately 290,000 extracted particles were subjected to 2D classification. Classes representing the STC were identified and used as templates for a second round of template-based particle picking, yielding approximately 1,000,000 particles that were re-subjected to 2D classification. The resulting 22,000 particles were used to train a Topaz neural network picking model (v0.2.5)52. After confirming model performance, additional particles were extracted from all micrographs using the trained model. The upcoming particle set underwent 2D classification, and selection of high-quality classes yielded 97,972 particles that were used for ab initio reconstruction. Heterogeneous refinement separated the dataset into two classes: 70,006 particles representing the STC complex and the remainder classified as non-particles. Non-uniform refinement of the STC class produced an initial map at 2.9 Å resolution. The particle stack was then subjected to 3D classification using principal component analysis with a 13 Å resolution cut-off, separating 18,831 particles lacking target DNA from 51,169 particles with target DNA bound. Both subsets were independently subjected to non-uniform refinement, yielding a 3.2 Å map for the STC without target DNA and a 2.9 Å map for the STC with target DNA. Both maps were further processed with DeepEMhancer v12132253 prior to model building.

According to recent reports, initial cryo-EM data collection on graphene grids revealed a strong preferred orientation bias, limiting the angular coverage of the dataset. To improve particle orientation distribution and enable higher-quality three-dimensional reconstructions, Ni-NTA lipid monolayer grids were subsequently prepared49.

A total of 144,294 movies were collected at a pixel size of 0.848 Å and processed using Patch Motion Correction and Patch CTF Estimation with a CTF-fit cut-off of less than 10 Å. Initial particle picking was performed by blob picking on approximately 2,600 micrographs, yielding ~570,000 extracted particles (binned 3×), which were subjected to two rounds of 2D classification to generate ~5,000 representative particles for training a Topaz neural network picking model (v0.2.5)52. The trained model was applied across all ~22,000 micrographs, extracting 2,722,447 particles (binned 3×). Following two rounds of 2D classification, 897,848 particles were retained for further analysis. The complete data processing workflow is described in Extended Data Fig. 4.

Recent findings suggest that single-particle analysis revealed substantial compositional heterogeneity within the reconstituted sample. Two-dimensional class averages resolved density for all expected components in multiple orientations (Extended Data Fig. 4). Heterogeneous refinement (n = 4) partitioned the dataset into 4 populations: 2 HIC classes (131,242 particles, 14.6%; and 462,255 particles, 54.8%), 1 STC–TnsC class (127,845 particles, 14.2%) and 1 Cascade class (146,705 particles, 16.4%). These populations enabled classification of the following assemblies: a Cascade–TniQ sub-complex (3.3 Å), a STC (2.9 Å) an STC–TnsC assembly (4.3 Å) and the complete HIC (4.5 Å) (Extended Data Fig. 4). Each population was further processed by sub-classification and homogeneous refinement. For the HIC, signal subtraction of the STC–TnsC region followed by 2D slice projection-guided particle sorting enabled focused local refinement, yielding a map at 4.5 Å resolution (Fourier shell correlation (FSC) = 0.143). Non-uniform refinement of the Cascade region within the full complex achieved 3.5 Å (FSC = 0.143). Free Cascade and Cascade–TniQ populations were resolved to 2.8 Å, 3.0 Å (closed) and 3.1 Å (open), respectively (FSC = 0.143). The HIC exhibits variable local resolution (3.7–9.0 Å, Supplementary Fig. 9), and focused refinements were combined into a composite map.

Recent findings suggest that for the STC maps, PDB 9Y7B was used as a starting model. The structure was initially docked into the STC-without-target-DNA map and manually rebuilt in Coot (v0.9.8.96)54 where required. DNA sequences were modified manually and fitted into the density using ISOLDE as a ChimeraX plugin (v1.11.1). The TnsA subunit was modelled using AlphaFold 3 and docked into the corresponding density. This assembled STC model was subsequently used as the starting model for the STC-with-target-DNA map. Structural rearrangements in TnsB required individual domains to be docked independently into the density before rejoining in Coot.

It has been revealed that for the Cascade–TniQ complex structures, individual Cas subunits were modelled using AlphaFold 3 and docked into the map. The DNA scaffold was derived from PDB 6PIJ and mutated to match the designed substrate sequence. The target recognition complex was assembled, and manual adjustments were performed in Coot.

Both the Cascade–TniQ and STC complex structures were used as starting models for modelling the HIC. TnsC protomers were individually modelled using AlphaFold 3 and docked into the density. The STC–TnsC portion of the HIC was used as the starting model for the off-pathway complex, with minor adjustments applied to the TnsC ring.

For all structures, real-space refinement of DNA substrates was performed in Phenix (v2.0rc1-5690)55 with base-pair and secondary structure restraints enforced. Model validation was carried out by computing map-model FSC at a 0.5 cut-off. The masked cross-correlation coefficient (CCmask) from refinement output was reported as the representative model-map cross-correlation. All validation statistics are summarized in Extended Data Table 1.

It has been revealed that helical rise and twist were measured from docked protomers in the HIC (PDB: 36AU) and VchTnsC structures (PDB: 7UFI) using a script from the Rosetta software suite: make_symmdef_file.pl56. Rise values (in Å) were extracted from the output and plotted using Python.

Liverpool are making moves, and this one is exciting.

It has been revealed that ronald Araujo has already been such a stalwart presence in the right-back role for the Reds. But the Uruguayan is merely a temporary solution.

According to recent reports, liverpool may exercise the option to buy him on a permanent transfer from Barcelona. However, long-term Araujo cannot be considered as the club's first choice right-back.

Industry observers note that he is a useful option to have. Someone who can really offer cover in multiple areas. But Liverpool need a proper right-back. A player capable of being a threat on the ball and go forward to create chances for his teammates.

Someone like Trent Alexander-Arnold.

It has been revealed that because the truth is Liverpool still haven't really replaced him. Jeremie Frimpong was never a serious consideration but more of a back-up option as well.

According to recent reports, when is Conor Bradley coming back for Liverpool?The initiative was to make the Northern Irishman the first-choice option for the Reds. Bradley was already competing with Alexander-Arnold for the right-back role, and he looked like he was ready to come in and be the first choice. But amid Trent's departure, Bradley had a tremendous amount of bad luck with injuries. He's now missed close to a year of football. Thankfully, he is on his way back. Bradley is training with the team and is making encouraging progress with his recovery. The Reds' medical staff are in no rush to bring him back straight away. They need to get him used to playing with the ball, physical contact and the rapid bursts of direction that football at such an elite level requires. It will still be a while until we see Bradley back looking like his old self.

SBV Excelsior vs Telstar - prediction, team news, lineups
